questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, passing from the middle cranial fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve exits via foramen rotundum.

questions.text: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the medulla oblongata, receiving input from the spinal cord and cerebral cortex and sending climbing fiber projections to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus: located in medulla oblongata.

questions.text: A patient has weakness of the right lower face, but can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Preserved forehead wrinkling indicates intact upper motor neuron (UMN) innervation to the facial nucleus's upper face region; weakness of only the lower face indicates a UMN lesion affecting the contralateral corticobulbar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Lower face weakness with spared forehead: contralateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesion.

questions.text: The muscle spindle is stretched by contraction of which fibres?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within the spindle, and when activated, they contract these fibers, stretching the sensory region and increasing spindle sensitivity to muscle stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons stretch intrafusal fibers, increasing muscle spindle sensitivity.

questions.text: The medial geniculate body is part of the auditory pathway and receives input from the:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus, serving as the thalamic relay for the auditory pathway to the auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body receives input from inferior colliculus.

questions.text: A patient with a tumour in the left frontal eye field (area 8) will have difficulty:
questions.explanation: The left frontal eye field (area 8) controls conjugate gaze to the right by sending signals that move both eyes rightward; a lesion here causes difficulty gazing to the contralateral (right) side.
questions.keyConcept: Left frontal eye field controls gaze to the right (contralateral).

questions.text: The sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the spinal cord at levels:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from T1 to L2 levels, representing the thoracolumbar outflow of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons: T1-L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).

questions.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) coordinates movements between which structures?
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects the vestibular nuclei to the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, coordinating eye movements with head movements in the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.keyConcept: MLF coordinates eyes and head via vestibulo-ocular reflex.

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The limbic system, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus, is fundamentally involved in emotional processing and memory formation, particularly through connections with the hypothalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic system: emotion and memory processing.
options: It is involved in emotion and memory.

questions.text: A patient has loss of pain and temperature on the right side of the body and loss of proprioception on the left side below the level of a spinal cord lesion. This pattern is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss (corticospinal and dorsal columns) below the lesion with contralateral pain/temperature loss (lateral spinothalamic crossing fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain loss below lesion.

questions.text: A patient develops contralateral loss of pain and temperature of the body with ipsilateral facial signs. The occluded vessel is the:
questions.explanation: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral pain and temperature loss below lesion: lateral spinothalamic tract lesion.
options: Superior cerebellar artery supplying the upper cerebellum

questions.text: Contralateral sensation from the face and body is represented in the:
questions.explanation: SI (areas 3,1,2) maps the contralateral half of the body and face.
questions.keyConcept: Face represented upside down in somatosensory cortex, with larger areas for lips and fingers.

questions.text: The motor branch to mylohyoid arises from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve as the:
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve gives the (motor) nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Motor branch to mylohyoid arises from posterior division of mandibular nerve (V3).

questions.text: The first-order neuron carrying pain and temperature from the face lies in the:
questions.explanation: Cell bodies are in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pain and temperature first-order neuron: pseudounipolar cell body in trigeminal ganglion.
options: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

questions.text: On the medial surface of the infratemporal fossa lies the:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid muscle lies on medial surface of infratemporal fossa.

questions.text: The chief retractor of the mandible is the:
questions.explanation: Posterior temporalis fibers retract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis is the chief retractor of mandible.

questions.text: The sensory (dorsal) part of the spinal cord develops from the:
questions.explanation: The alar plate forms sensory (dorsal) grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory dorsal horn develops from alar lamina of neural tube.

questions.text: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb (elbow/wrist) is carried by the:
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from upper limb to cerebellum.

questions.text: A patient shows ipsilateral tongue atrophy, contralateral loss of vibration, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature of the body. The lesion is in the:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII, medial lemniscus, pyramid).
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviation toward lesion with ipsilateral atrophy: hypoglossal nerve lesion.

questions.text: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from a "danger area" facial infection spreads via the:
questions.explanation: Facial vein to superior ophthalmic vein to cavernous sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial infection: danger area around nose/upper lip.
options: Inferior petrosal sinus to the IJV

questions.text: Retrolentiform part of internal capsule DOESN'T transmit:
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of internal capsule contains visual radiation, occipito-pontine, and parieto-pontine fibers, but the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform: visual/occipito-parieto-pontine fibers; auditory goes sublentiform.

questions.text: The superior speech center is situated within the ……… area.
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA, medial area 6) is the superior speech center involved in planning and initiating speech movements, lying medial to premotor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Superior speech center: supplementary motor area.

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the speech areas:
questions.explanation: Speech areas are typically asymmetric; Broca's and Wernicke's areas are usually dominant in one hemisphere (left in right-handers), not equally present in both.
questions.keyConcept: Speech areas are not present equally in both hemispheres.
options: Motor area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Sensory area lies in parietal and temporal lobes.
Sensory area is concerned with understanding visual and auditory information.
Both areas are present in both cerebral hemispheres.

questions.text: Choose the correct statement about the sensory homunculus:
questions.explanation: The sensory homunculus represents the body upside-down (inverted) in the postcentral gyrus, with larger representations for areas with higher receptor density like lips and fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory homunculus: body represented upside-down in postcentral gyrus.
options: It is the body representation within the motor cortex.
Somatosensory cortex corresponds point by point with regions in ipsilateral side of the body.
The body is represented upside down.
The body representation depends on the size of the target part.

questions.text: Posterior choroidal artery is a branch from ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The posterior choroidal artery is a branch of the posterior cerebral artery that supplies the choroid plexus of the lateral and third ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior choroidal artery: branch of posterior cerebral artery.

questions.text: Inability to perform tasks although the person has the will to perform it indicates a lesion in ……… area.
questions.explanation: A premotor area lesion causes apraxia - inability to perform tasks despite intact motor pathways and will, due to loss of motor planning programs.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor lesion: apraxia (can't perform tasks despite will).

questions.text: Inability to recognize familiar objects by touch indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) results from lesions in the superior parietal lobule, which integrates sensory information for object recognition.
questions.keyConcept: Astereognosis: superior parietal lobule lesion.

questions.text: Which of the following is mesodermal in origin?
questions.explanation: Dura mater is derived from mesoderm (specifically the paraxial mesoderm surrounding the neural tube), while arachnoid and pia mater are ectodermal derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: mesodermal origin.

questions.text: The anterior neuropore of neural tube closes at ……… day of pregnancy.
questions.explanation: The anterior neuropore closes at day 25 of embryonic development; failure results in anencephaly. The posterior neuropore closes around day 27.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior neuropore closes at day 25 of pregnancy.

questions.text: Myelination inside the CNS depends on:
questions.explanation: Myelination in the CNS is performed by oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelination: oligodendrocytes (PNS: Schwann cells).

questions.text: Regarding the development of the spinal cord, choose the incorrect combination:
questions.explanation: The alar lamina (sensory) forms the dorsal horns of grey matter, while the basal lamina (motor) forms the ventral horns - the statement incorrectly matches them.
questions.keyConcept: Alar lamina: dorsal horns; Basal lamina: ventral horns.
options: The lumen of the neural tube – the central canal.
The alar lamina – the ventral horns of the grey matter.
Neurons opposite the sulcus limitans – lateral horns of the grey matter.
The marginal layer – the white matter.

questions.text: The neural crest gives all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Spinal nerves are formed from dorsal and ventral roots which originate from the neural tube (CNS), not from neural crest. Neural crest gives dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, and postganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerves: from neural tube, not neural crest.

questions.text: Failure of closure of the neural tube leads to:
questions.explanation: Rachischisis (myeloschisis) results from failure of neural tube closure, causing exposure of neural tissue; spina bifida results from vertebral arch defects.
questions.keyConcept: Neural tube closure failure: rachischisis (exposed neural tissue).

questions.text: The adult derivatives of the telencephalon are:
questions.explanation: The telencephalon develops into the cerebral hemispheres including the basal ganglia, hippocampus, and lateral ventricles, while thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain derive from diencephalon and mesencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres.

questions.text: The cavity of the mesencephalon is:
questions.explanation: The cavity of the mesencephalon is the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalon cavity: cerebral aqueduct.

questions.text: Match the cortical area in column A with the result of lesion in column B.
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area lesion: word comprehension loss; primary auditory: decreased hearing; secondary auditory: sound understanding; frontal eye field: voluntary gaze loss; primary visual: hemianopia with macular sparing.
questions.keyConcept: Lesion effects: Wernicke (comprehension), 1ary auditory (hearing), 2ary auditory (sound meaning), eye field (gaze), 1ary visual (hemianopia).

pairs.target: Inability to understand written or spoken words.
Loss of voluntary conjugate eye movement.

questions.text: The occipitofrontalis muscle accounts for the ……… layer of the scalp.
questions.explanation: The occipitofrontalis muscle forms the third (musculoaponeurotic) layer of the scalp, connecting the galea aponeurotica to the orbital margins.
questions.keyConcept: Occipitofrontalis: third layer of scalp.

questions.text: Skin of the hairy area of the temple is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) supplies the hairy temple area, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular division.
questions.keyConcept: Hairy temple: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

questions.text: The great auricular nerve carries fibers from:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from C2-C3 ventral rami (cervical plexus) and supplies the skin of the ear and adjacent scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve: C2 and C3 ventral rami.

questions.text: Skin over occipital bone up to the vertex is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The posterior primary rami of C2 and C3 supply the skin over the occipital bone up to the vertex, including the greater and lesser occipital nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Occipital area: supplied by dorsal rami of C2 and C3.

questions.text: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of ……… veins.
questions.explanation: The anterior facial vein is formed by union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins at the medial angle of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior facial vein: formed by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins.

questions.text: The common facial vein drains into the ……… vein.
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein after forming from the facial and anterior facial veins joining.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein: drains into internal jugular vein.

questions.text: A muscle covered by deep fascia is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is covered by thebuccal fascia (deep fascia), while orbicularis oculi and oris are covered by superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: covered by deep fascia (buccal fascia).

questions.text: A muscle develops from the first pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: Masseter develops from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage), along with other muscles of mastication and mylohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter: first pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the orbicularis oculi muscle:
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches behind the lacrimal sac (posterior to it), not in front, to compress and dilate the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi lacrimal part: attached behind lacrimal sac.
options: Its orbital part closes the eye tightly.
Its palpebral part closes the eye gently.
Its lacrimal part is attached in front of the lacrimal sac.
It develops from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.text: An active muscle during whistling is:
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle compresses and purses the lips during whistling, while buccinator muscle keeps food between teeth during chewing.
questions.keyConcept: Whistling: orbicularis oris contracts to purse lips.

questions.text: Accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth denotes weakness of ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: Buccinator weakness causes food accumulation in the vestibule because this muscle normally keeps food between the teeth during mastication.
questions.keyConcept: Food in vestibule: buccinator weakness.

questions.text: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and lower ear region as part of cervical plexus distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Angle of mandible: great auricular nerve (C2-C3).

questions.text: Pain from the lower eyelid is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (V2) carries pain sensation from the lower eyelid, upper lip, and cheek, exiting through the infraorbital foramen on the anterior maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower eyelid pain: infraorbital nerve (V2).

questions.text: Infection in the area of chin leads to enlargement of ……… lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes drain the chin and lower lip midline, lying beneath the chin in the submental triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Chin infection: submental lymph nodes enlarge.

questions.text: The dural fold which is attached to the skull vault is:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.

questions.text: Ethmoidal arteries supply the cranial dura via ……… arteries.
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) give off anterior meningeal arteries that supply the cranial dura in the anterior fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Ethmoidal arteries supply dura via anterior meningeal branches.

questions.text: All the following are true about the middle meningeal artery EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.
options: It is the largest meningeal artery.
It is a branch from 1st part of maxillary artery.
It enters the cranial cavity through foramen ovale.
It gives frontal and parietal terminal branches.

questions.text: It is not a must to test the ……… nerve in case of cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits via stylomastoid foramen, so it wouldn't be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve not in cavernous sinus, so not tested in thrombosis.

questions.text: The cavernous sinus is drained to the transverse sinus by ……… sinus.
questions.explanation: The superior petrosal sinus drains the cavernous sinus into the transverse sinus, running along the petrous ridge at the attachment of tentorium cerebelli.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains to transverse sinus via superior petrosal sinus.

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the straight sinus:
questions.explanation: The straight sinus deviates to the LEFT to continue as the left transverse sinus (not right); the right transverse sinus typically continues from the superior sagittal sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Straight sinus deviates LEFT to become left transverse sinus.
options: It is formed by union of inferior sagittal sinus and great cerebral vein.
Runs in the junction between falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.
Deviates to the right to continue as the right transverse sinus.
It is connected to the confluence of sinuses.

questions.text: Which of the following diploic veins drains extracranially?
questions.explanation: The frontal diploic vein drains through the supraorbital notch to the supraorbital vein and eventually the angular vein, providing extracranial drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal diploic vein drains extracranially via supraorbital vein.

questions.text: All the following are tributaries of external jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein, not the external jugular. The external jugular tributaries are anterior jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular, and posterior external jugular.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains internal jugular, not external jugular.

questions.text: The only tributary of the subclavian vein is:
questions.explanation: The external jugular vein is the only named tributary of the subclavian vein, carrying blood from the superficial structures of the head and neck.
questions.keyConcept: External jugular vein: only named tributary of subclavian vein.

questions.text: The viscera of the neck are surrounded by ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath around the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid gland, fusing laterally with the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia surrounds cervical viscera.

questions.text: The retropharyngeal space lies:
questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering pharynx/esophagus) anteriorly and prevertebral fascia posteriorly, extending from skull base to T1.
questions.keyConcept: Retropharyngeal space: between buccopharyngeal and prevertebral fascia.

questions.text: The axillary sheath is an extension from ……… fascia.
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is an extension of the prevertebral fascia (from the anterior vertebral muscles) that surrounds the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Axillary sheath: extension of prevertebral fascia.

questions.text: An infrahyoid muscle supplied directly by C1 ventral ramus is:
questions.explanation: The thyrohyoid muscle is innervated directly by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, while other infrahyoid muscles receive ansa cervicalis (C1-3).
questions.keyConcept: Thyrohyoid: directly by C1 via hypoglossal nerve.

questions.text: A branch from external carotid artery running in both carotid and digastric triangles is ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The facial artery runs through both carotid triangle (origin from ECA) and digastric triangle (before entering face), giving off branches like submental, superior labial, and lateral nasal.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery: runs through both carotid and digastric triangles.

questions.text: The carotid sheath encloses:
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve throughout its course in the neck.
questions.keyConcept: Carotid sheath: contains CCA/ICA, IJV, and vagus nerve.

questions.text: A nerve running along the posterior border of sternomastoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve runs along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle, arising from C2 ventral ramus to supply the scalp behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve: posterior border of SCM.

questions.text: The subclavian artery is divided into 3 parts by ……… muscle.
questions.explanation: The anterior scalene muscle divides the subclavian artery into three parts: first (posterior to scalene), second (behind scalene), and third (lateral to scalene).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery divided by anterior scalene muscle into 3 parts.

questions.text: A nerve embedded in the roof of the posterior triangle of the neck and crossing the triangle parallel to levator scapulae is:
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle embedded in its roof, running from the sternocleidomastoid to the trapezius, parallel to levator scapulae.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve: crosses posterior triangle parallel to levator scapulae.

questions.text: Tight scalene muscles can compress:
questions.explanation: Tight scalene muscles (especially anterior and middle) can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus in the costoclavicular space, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Scalene tightness compresses subclavian artery.

questions.text: A nerve related to anterior aspect of anterior scalene muscle is:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve runs on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle, making it vulnerable during scalene blocks and relevant in interscalene anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Phrenic nerve: anterior aspect of anterior scalene muscle.

questions.text: A muscle DOESN'T share in boundaries of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The rectus capitis posterior minor does NOT form boundaries of the suboccipital triangle - only rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior do.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle: rectus major, obliquus superior/inferior (NOT rectus minor).

questions.text: A nerve seen in the floor of the suboccipital triangle is:
questions.explanation: The dorsal ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve) emerges in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, providing motor innervation to suboccipital muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Suboccipital triangle floor: dorsal ramus of C1.

questions.text: Which of the following lies superficial to temporalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve lies superficial to the temporalis fascia as it ascends toward the temple, carrying sensory fibers from the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve: superficial to temporalis fascia.

questions.text: A muscle acting as a powerful retractor of the mandible is:
questions.explanation: The temporalis muscle is a powerful retractor of the mandible, pulling the mandibular condyle backward to close the mouth after opening.
questions.keyConcept: Temporalis: powerful retractor of mandible.

questions.text: The main opener of the mouth is:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid is the main mouth opener, pulling the mandibular neck forward and down; gravity and suprahyoid muscles assist.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid: main opener of mouth.

questions.text: The mandibular nerve reaches the infratemporal fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) passes from the middle cranial fossa to the infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve enters infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.

questions.text: The trunk of the mandibular nerve supplies ……… muscle(s).
questions.explanation: The trunk of the mandibular nerve gives off medial pterygoid nerve (supplying medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palati) before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
questions.keyConcept: V3 trunk supplies: medial pterygoid, tensor tympani, tensor palati.

questions.text: Middle meningeal artery is encircled by roots of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve encircles the middle meningeal artery with its two roots, forming a neural loop around the vessel in the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve encircles middle meningeal artery.

questions.text: Bad extraction of lower 3rd molar tooth may cause loss of sensations from:
questions.explanation: Bad extraction of lower third molar can damage the inferior alveolar nerve (running in the mandibular canal), causing anesthesia of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 3rd molar extraction: possible lingual nerve damage (anterior 2/3 tongue).

questions.text: To operate on the lower teeth, the ……… nerve is anaesthetized.
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) is anesthetized for lower teeth operations, injected near the mandibular foramen on the medial aspect of the ramus.
questions.keyConcept: Lower teeth surgery: inferior alveolar nerve anesthetized.

questions.text: A branch from the 3rd part of maxillary artery is:
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar artery is a branch of the third part of maxillary artery that supplies the upper molars and sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior superior alveolar artery: branch of maxillary artery part 3.

questions.text: A nerve passing between the 2 heads of lateral pterygoid muscle is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle to reach the buccinator muscle, carrying sensory and motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve passes between two heads of lateral pterygoid.

questions.text: Fracture of neck of mandible can lead to injury of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve runs on the lateral surface of the mandibular neck, so it can be injured in fractures; the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves are also at risk, but auriculotemporal is not typically affected.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular neck fracture: masseteric, lingual, inferior alveolar nerves at risk.

questions.text: Maxillary nerve reaches the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) passes from the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve reaches pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum.

questions.text: Pain from upper canine teeth is carried by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The upper canine teeth are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of infraorbital nerve, V2), which also supplies the upper incisors.
questions.keyConcept: Upper canine: anterior superior alveolar nerve (V2).

questions.text: The skin of the prominence of cheek is supplied by ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the skin over the cheek prominence (zygomatic area), a branch of V2 via the zygomatic nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cheek prominence: zygomaticotemporal nerve (V2).

questions.text: Nerve of pterygoid canal is formed by union of ……… nerves.
questions.explanation: The nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidians nerve) is formed by the union of the greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic from CN VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic from carotid plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Nerve of pterygoid canal: greater petrosal + deep petrosal nerves.

questions.text: Deviation of the uvula to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Uvula deviation to the right indicates right motor nucleus of vagus (CN X) damage (NMN lesion causing ipsilateral palatine muscle paralysis), since the uvula moves away from the paralyzed side.
questions.keyConcept: Uvula deviates AWAY from lesioned side (CN X motor).

questions.text: Reflex cough accompanying ear wash is caused by irritation of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve) innervates the external acoustic meatus; its irritation during ear washing triggers the cough reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Ear wash cough reflex: auricular branch of vagus nerve.

questions.text: The jugular foramen transmits all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, and the inferior petrosal sinus; the spinal accessory root (descending from foramen magnum) also passes through but the hypoglossal canal is separate.
questions.keyConcept: Jugular foramen: CN 9,10,11, inferior petrosal sinus (not hypoglossal).

questions.text: Difficulty in protruding the tongue with its deviation to the right side denotes injury of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: Tongue deviation toward the right side during protrusion indicates right hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, as the unaffected genioglossus pulls the tongue toward the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Tongue deviates TOWARD lesioned hypoglossal nerve side.

questions.text: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion is the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII carrying parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands).
questions.keyConcept: Submandibular ganglion parasympathetic root: chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.text: The ……… nerve suspends the pterygopalatine ganglion in its place.
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended by the maxillary nerve (V2) which provides its sensory roots passing through without synapsing.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve suspends pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.text: A branch from the 2nd part of subclavian artery is:
questions.explanation: The second part of subclavian artery gives rise to the internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk (supplying thyroid, neck, and chest wall structures).
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian artery part 2: internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk.

questions.text: The common carotid artery divides at the level of ……… vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4), becoming ICA and ECA.
questions.keyConcept: Common carotid bifurcates at upper border of thyroid cartilage (C4).

questions.text: The external carotid artery crosses ……… triangles of the neck.
questions.explanation: The external carotid artery runs through the carotid triangle after originating in the neck, with branches emerging from its anterior, posterior, and medial surfaces.
questions.keyConcept: External carotid crosses carotid triangle of neck.

questions.text: All the following drain into the internal jugular vein EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein; other veins like inferior thyroid, middle thyroid, and vertebral vein also drain into the IJV.
questions.keyConcept: Common facial vein drains INTO internal jugular (so it doesn't drain external jugular).

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the subclavian vein:
questions.explanation: The subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to the anterior scalene muscle (not posterior), making it vulnerable to compression during clavicle fractures.
questions.keyConcept: Subclavian vein lies ANTERIOR to anterior scalene.
options: It is the continuation of the axillary vein.
It is separated from subclavian artery by anterior scalene muscle.
It grooves the 1st rib posterior to scalene tubercle.
It receives the external jugular vein.

questions.text: An abscess in the center of lower lip may cause enlargement of ……… lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: An abscess in the lower lip drains to the submandibular lymph nodes due to lymphatic drainage patterns of the anterior face.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip abscess: submandibular lymph nodes enlarge.

questions.text: One of the following mandibular ligaments is a remnant of cartilage of the 1st pharyngeal arch:
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament is the remnant of Meckels cartilage (first pharyngeal arch cartilage), stretching from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament: remnant of 1st pharyngeal arch cartilage.

questions.text: Rotation of the head to say "No" occurs at ……… joint.
questions.explanation: The atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2) allows head rotation for saying no through the dens-articular facet articulation.
questions.keyConcept: Saying no: rotation at atlanto-axial joint (C1-C2).

questions.text: A muscle develops from the pharyngeal arch is:
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle develops from the second pharyngeal arch (like other muscles of facial expression), innervated by the facial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator: second pharyngeal arch derivative.

questions.text: The lower lip is derived from:
questions.explanation: The lower lip is derived from the mandibular prominence (frontonasal process gives upper lip philtrum and maxilla), with lateral portions from the maxillary prominence.
questions.keyConcept: Lower lip: derived from mandibular prominence.

questions.text: The inter-maxillary segment gives all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (primary palate) gives rise to the premaxilla, primary palate, and four incisor teeth; the secondary palate forms from palatine shelves.
questions.keyConcept: Intermaxillary segment: premaxilla, primary palate, incisors (NOT secondary palate).
options: Sockets of the upper 4 incisor teeth.

questions.text: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from ……… prominence.
questions.explanation: The upper part of the cheeks is derived from the maxillary prominence (second pharyngeal arch), which also forms the upper lip lateral portions and secondary palate.
questions.keyConcept: Upper cheek: maxillary prominence.

questions.text: Excessive fusion between maxillary and mandibular prominences causes:
questions.explanation: Fusion of maxillary and mandibular prominences in utero causes microstomia (small mouth) or aglossia (absent tongue) if severe.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary-mandibular fusion: microstomia or aglossia.

questions.text: Abnormal early closure of coronal suture leads to:
questions.explanation: Early closure of the coronal suture causes brachycephaly (shortened anteroposterior skull diameter) due to compensatory growth in other directions.
questions.keyConcept: Coronal suture early closure: brachycephaly.

questions.text: Match the muscle in column A with its main action in column B.
questions.explanation: Matching pairs: Masseter elevates mandible, Temporalis retracts mandible, Medial pterygoid elevates and protrudes, Lateral pterygoid protrudes and opens, Digastric opens mouth, Buccinator compresses cheeks.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle actions: masseter elevate, temporalis retract, pterygoids protrude, digastric open, buccinator compress.

pairs.target: B) Lateral flexion of the skull.

questions.text: As regards the histological structure of gray matter of spinal cord, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Nerve fibers within the gray matter are mostly unmyelinated or thinly myelinated, not heavily myelinated. Heavy myelination is characteristic of white matter tracts. The gray matter contains neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and glial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Gray matter fibers are mostly unmyelinated; white matter fibers are myelinated
options: It contain nerve cells & neuroglia cells.
The nerve fibers within the gray matter are mostly myelinated.
Golgi type II neurons terminate in gray matter near their origin.
Golgi type I neurons form long ascending fibers.

questions.text:
Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
I. Pacinian corpuscle.
II. Meissner’s corpuscle.
III. Ruffini’ corpuscle.
questions.explanation: Ruffini's corpuscles (type II slowly adapting mechanoreceptors) are proprioceptors in joints and skin. Pacinian corpuscles are vibration/pressure receptors. Meissner's corpuscles are light touch in dermal papillae. Muscle spindles are the primary proprioceptors in muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors: muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, Ruffini's (joints). Vibration: Pacinian. Light touch: Meissner's.

questions.text: Which of the following is a receptor for vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles (type V rapidly adapting) are the primary vibration and deep pressure receptors. They are located deep in the dermis and respond to high-frequency vibration. Meissner's is light touch, Ruffini's is stretch, Merkel's is pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: vibration (500 Hz), deep pressure, rapidly adapting, deep dermis.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a character of Meissner’s corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscle has Schwann cells arranged in horizontal stacks (not spirally). The nerve fiber runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks. Merkel's disc has nerve fibers running spirally. Meissner's is encapsulated, in dermal papillae, and responds to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: Schwann cells in horizontal stacks, nerve fibers spiral; light touch receptor in dermal papillae.
options: It is an encapsulated nerve ending.
It is present in dermal papillae.
The Schwann cells are arranged in two cores.
The nerve fibers run spirally between the Schwann cells.

questions.text: All about muscle spindle true except:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen fibers primarily). The capsule encloses the spindle but the internal structure is muscle fiber-based. They are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, have gamma efferents, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel with extrafusal fibers, contains intrafusal muscle fibers, encapsulated, gamma innervation.
options: Present in parallel with sk. Muscle fibers.

questions.text: Krause end bulb, all true except:
questions.explanation: Krause end bulbs have spherical structures with a gelatinous core, function as cold receptors, and are found in conjunctiva and oral cavity. They are mechanoreceptors. The statement about flattened Teloglia cells is incorrect - they have a different structure.
questions.keyConcept: Krause end bulb: cold receptor, mechanoreceptor, gelatinous core, found in conjunctiva and mouth.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of muscle spindle:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are innervated by both afferent (Ia, II) and efferent (gamma) nerve fibers. They contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen), are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, respond to stretch, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel arrangement, intrafusal fibers, afferent + efferent innervation, stretch receptor.
options: Present In series with muscle fibers.
Innervated by afferent & efferent nerve fiber.

questions.text: Pacinian corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric layers of Teloglia (not Schwann cells arranged transversely). They are located deep in the dermis (not dermal papillae), are encapsulated (not non-capsulated), and the nerve fiber runs centrally (not in spiral).
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: concentric Teloglia layers, deep dermis, vibration receptor, encapsulated.
options: Lies in dermal papillae of skin.
Nerve fibers run in spiral coarse.

questions.text: Which of the following receptors are mechanoreceptors?
questions.explanation: All of these - Merkel's disc, Meissner's corpuscle, and Bounet's plexus (a free nerve ending network) are mechanoreceptors. They transduce mechanical stimuli into neural signals. Merkel's = pressure, Meissner's = light touch, Bounet's = slowly adapting stretch receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanoreceptors: Merkel's (pressure), Meissner's (touch), Bounet's plexus (stretch). All detect mechanical stimuli.

questions.text: The sensory nerve enters the Meissner’s corpuscle from:
questions.explanation: In Meissner's corpuscle, the sensory nerve enters from the SIDE (laterally), not from the lower part or central core. The nerve fiber then runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks within the corpuscle.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: sensory nerve enters from side; nerve fibers spiral between Schwann cell stacks.

questions.text: Free nerve endings are widely distributed in
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are the simplest sensory receptors and are widely distributed throughout the body including epidermis, cornea, mucous membranes of visceral organs, and serous membranes. They detect pain, temperature, and crude touch.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: most widely distributed receptor; detect pain, temperature, crude touch; in epidermis, cornea, viscera.

questions.text: What do free nerve endings respond to?
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings respond to noxious (painful), thermal, and crude touch stimuli. They are polymodal receptors capable of detecting multiple stimulus types. Different fiber types (A-delta for pain/temperature, C for pain) mediate these responses.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: polymodal - respond to painful, thermal, and tactile stimuli via Aδ and C fibers.

questions.text: What is the site of Merkel’s tactile disc?
questions.explanation: Merkel's tactile discs are found in BOTH hairy and non-hairy skin, particularly in the deep layers of epidermis of palms, soles, and at transitional zones between hairy and non-hairy skin. They are slowly adapting touch receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Merkel's disc: deep epidermis of palms/soles and hairy-non hairy skin transitions; slowly adapting touch receptor.
options: Deep layers of the epidermis of the palmer surfaces of hands and planter surfaces of feet
Transitional sites between hairy & non-hairy skin

questions.text: Pacinian corpuscles are found in
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are found in deep tissues including dermis and hypodermis, as well as mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder, and other viscera. They detect deep pressure and vibration. Their wide distribution reflects their role in detecting deep mechanical stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles: deep dermis, hypodermis, mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder - deep pressure/vibration.

questions.text: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lumbar spinal cord has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains a large amount of grey matter (lower motor neurons for legs) relative to white matter (mostly descending tracts passing through). It has lateral horns for sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar cord: large grey matter (LMN for lower limb), small white/grey ratio, lateral horns present.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of thoracic level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The thoracic spinal cord has 4 horns (anterior, posterior, and lateral on each side). The lateral horns contain sympathetic preganglionic neurons. It is intermediate in size, oval-shaped. Cervical and lumbar enlargements are larger.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic cord: 4 horns including lateral horns (sympathetic), intermediate size, oval shape.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has the LARGEST white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains extensive ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) tracts to/from the brain for the upper limbs and body. It is rounded in shape and large in size.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord: largest white/grey ratio (many tracts), rounded, large size.
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio

questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion:
questions.explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.text: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
questions.explanation: DRG cells are pseudounipolar with multiple processes (one peripheral, one central). They have eccentric nuclei, are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers, and are surrounded by satellite glial cells (not Schwann cells around the cell body itself).
questions.keyConcept: DRG cells: pseudounipolar, multiple processes, eccentric nucleus, satellite cells, myelinated + unmyelinated fibers.
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.
Have shwann cells around its cell bodies.

questions.text:
Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
I. It is rich in connective tissue cells.
II. It is soft jelly like.
III. It has grey matter and white matter.
questions.explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft, jelly-like (due to high water content), and has both grey matter (cell bodies) and white matter (myelinated fibers).
questions.keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.

questions.text: Dura matter characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Dura mater is a fibrous, avascular layer (contains few blood vessels). It forms the outermost meninx. Arachnoid has trabeculae; pia is vascular; arachnoid barrier layer is cellular. Dura's toughness comes from collagen fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: tough outer meninx, fibrous, relatively avascular; attached to periosteum of skull/vertebrae.

questions.text: Concerning the pia matter, which of the following statements is true:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is highly vascular (contains blood vessels that penetrate to supply superficial brain tissue). It is the innermost meninx, in direct contact with brain. Arachnoid contains spaces (subarachnoid) for CSF, not pia. Dura contains venous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater: highly vascular, innermost meninx, follows brain contours closely.

questions.text: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (in grey matter) have numerous short branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (in white matter) have few long unbranched processes. Both types express GFAP and have foot processes on blood vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: grey matter, numerous short processes. Fibrous astrocytes: white matter, few long processes.

questions.text: Tanycytes line which of the following:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the third ventricle and other ventricular surfaces, particularly in the hypothalamus. They have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and are involved in neuroendocrine regulation.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes: specialized ependymal cells lining 3rd ventricle, transport molecules between brain and CSF.

questions.text: The apical surface of ependymal Cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.

questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated. This ependymal lining continues throughout the ventricular system. The cilia help circulate CSF within the canal.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal: lined by partially ciliated simple columnar-cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells).
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ___ while microglia Is derived from ___:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (neural tube/glial precursors), same as neurons and astrocytes. Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage), making them the only non-ectodermal glial cells in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: neuroectoderm. Microglia: mesoderm (monocyte origin). Astrocytes: neuroectoderm.

questions.text: Which of the following cells Produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons). Schwann cells do this in the PNS. Astrocytes provide support; satellite cells support neurons in ganglia; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (multiple axons). Schwann cells: PNS myelin (one axon each).

questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in injury and disease to phagocytose debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages (phagocytic), mesodermal origin, activated in injury/disease.

questions.text: In the CNS Injury, which of the following cells are abundant:
questions.explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.
questions.keyConcept: CNS injury response: astrocyte proliferation (gliosis) + microglia activation (phagocytosis).

questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes (specifically their foot processes) are key components of the blood-brain barrier, forming a protective layer around capillaries. They induce endothelial cells to form tight junctions. Ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier, not BBB.
questions.keyConcept: Blood-brain barrier: astrocyte foot processes + tight junction endothelial cells; excludes many substances.

questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter appears grey because it contains nerve cell bodies (unmyelinated or lightly myelinated). White matter appears white due to myelin on axons. The distribution of myelin determines the distribution of grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter: neuron cell bodies. White matter: myelinated axons. Myelin determines white/grey distribution.

questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies, glial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of WHITE matter, not grey matter. This is why grey matter appears grey (neuron cell bodies) and white matter appears white (myelin).
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter: cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated fibers. White matter: myelinated axons.

questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
questions.keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.

questions.text: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) arranged in a thin connective tissue layer. It is not epithelial (not squamous or columnar). The outer surface faces the subarachnoid space, and the inner surface is in contact with brain.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater: modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal CT), highly vascular, innermost meninx.

questions.text: tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the brain-CSF barrier, limiting passage between ventricles and brain parenchyma. The blood-brain barrier involves astrocyte foot processes and tight junction endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal tight junctions = brain-CSF barrier. Astrocyte foot processes + endothelial tight junctions = blood-brain barrier.

questions.text: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein specific to astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in histology and neuropathology. Oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells do not contain GFAP.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP: astrocyte marker (intermediate filament). Used to identify astrocytes in CNS.

questions.text: Climbing fibers:
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers are the axons of contralateral inferior olivary nucleus neurons. They ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and climb on Purkinje cell dendrites. They carry error signals for motor learning. Mossy fibers (not climbing) end in granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers: olivocerebellar (contralateral ION), climb on Purkinje dendrites, carry error signals.

questions.text: The outer band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL GRANULAR layer (layer IV). This band represents dense termination of thalamocortical fibers. The inner band of Baillarger is in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V).
questions.keyConcept: Outer Baillarger: layer IV (internal granular) - thalamocortical input. Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal).

questions.text: The inner band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The inner band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V), which contains Betz cells in the motor cortex and other pyramidal neurons. The horizontal myelinated fibers form this band.
questions.keyConcept: Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal) - contains Betz cells and corticospinal neurons.

questions.text: The cytoplasm of astrocytes contains
questions.explanation: Astrocytes contain microtubules (for transport), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein - their intermediate filament marker), and thread-like mitochondria. These contents help identify astrocytes histologically. GFAP is the most specific marker.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte cytoplasm: GFAP (marker), microtubules, mitochondria. GFAP used for astrocyte identification.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about microglia?
questions.explanation: Microglia are present in CNS including retina and optic nerve (CNS outgrowths). They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles and fine spines on their surfaces. They are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages, spindle-shaped with branched spiny processes, mesodermal origin.
options: They are present in the retina and optic nerve
They are small spindle shaped cells with branching poles
The cell body and processes have minute spines on their surfaces

questions.text: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
questions.explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the ARCUATE NUCLEUS (not the cuneate nucleus which projects to cerebellum via dorsal external arcuate fibers). The arcuate nucleus receives corticofugal fibers and projects to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate: from arcuate nucleus → cerebellum (via ICP). Dorsal external arcuate: from accessory cuneate → cerebellum.

questions.text: Accessory cuneate nucleus give rise to:
questions.explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.

questions.text: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:
questions.explanation: The central gray (around the central canal) in the upper closed medulla contains the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. At this level, it is continuous with the spinal nucleus in the medulla. The nucleus solitarius is more lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Central gray upper medulla: spinal nucleus of V. More laterally: nucleus solitarius. Ventrally: inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.

questions.text: Inferior olivary nucleus:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers). It is located in the OPEN medulla, not ventral aspect. Its efferent fibers decussate and reach the CONTRALATERAL cerebellar cortex through the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle as climbing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary: receives rubral input, in open medulla, projects via ICP to contralateral cerebellum as climbing fibers.
options: Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mousy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.

questions.text: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract. Fibers from the superior colliculus cross in the dorsal tegmentum at the inferior colliculus level to descend and control neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level.

questions.text: The ventral tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL tegmental decussation is formed by the RUBROSPINAL tract. Fibers from the red nucleus cross in the midbrain (at superior colliculus level) to descend and control limb flexor muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral tegmental decussation: rubrospinal tract crosses at superior colliculus level.

questions.text: Mention the cutaneous unencapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous unencapsulated receptors include free nerve endings (pain, temperature), peritrichial endings around hair follicles (light touch), and Merkel's discs (fine touch); all lack a connective tissue capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Unencapsulated cutaneous receptors

questions.text: Mention the cutaneous encapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous encapsulated receptors include Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (vibration), Ruffini endings (stretch), and Merkel's discs are sometimes considered encapsulated; all have a surrounding connective tissue capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Encapsulated cutaneous receptors

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has an oval/rounded shape in cross-section due to the enlargement from C5-T1 segments (brachial plexus innervation). The white matter/grey matter ratio increases caudally, not cranially.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical spinal cord is rounded/oval in shape due to cervical enlargement
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio.

questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of variable size (both large light and small dark neurons), not uniform size. The large cells give off heavily myelinated fibers for proprioception; small cells give off lightly myelinated fibers for pain/temperature.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - FALSE
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp.
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion?
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.text: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
questions.explanation: DRG neurons have variable sizes, multiple processes (bipolar or pseudounipolar), and are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers. They do not all have the same size, and the nucleus is typically central, not eccentric.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable size, multiple processes, both myelinated/unmyelinated fibers
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.

questions.text: Nucleus dorsalis (Claris nucleus), all true except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (not ventral), located in lamina VII at C8-L3 levels. It has large cells with central nucleus, not eccentric nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus gives rise to DORSAL spinocerebellar tract (not ventral) - FALSE
options: In the medial aspect of the base of the posterior horn, in level from C8-L3.
Involved in lamina 7 of gray matter.
Give rise to ventral spinocerebellar tract.

questions.text: One of the following nuclei is not present in all segments of the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the nucleus dorsalis of Clark is TRUE?
questions.explanation: The nucleus dorsalis of Clark projects to the cerebellum via the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, carrying proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and tendon organs. It is in the dorsal horn, present only at certain levels (C8-L3).
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus projects to cerebellum via dorsal spinocerebellar tract
options: It is found in the ventral horn.
It is present at all spinal levels.
It is homologous in function to the main sensory nucleus.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the lateral horn of the spinal cord is TRUE?
questions.explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels
options: Gives origin to pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers.
It is most prominent at sacral levels.
It is present in all spinal cord levels.

questions.text: Destruction of the ventral horn results in one of the following:
questions.explanation: Destruction of the ventral horn (lower motor neuron) causes flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy, loss of reflexes, and fasciculations. Crude touch (dorsal column), fine touch (dorsal column), and pain sensation (spinothalamic) are not affected.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral horn destruction causes flaccid paralysis (LMN lesion)

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the grey matter?
questions.explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)
options: It is located outside the white matter in spinal cord.
It is formed of nerve cells mainly.
It has satellite cells sheath around its cells.

questions.text: Anterior horn of spinal cord contains the following nuclei EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei (the latter two at different cord levels). There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn - that description is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei: anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral (no 'middle' nucleus) - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are present in lamina «.. of spinal cord gray matter:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, corresponding to lamina VII of Rexed. Parasympathetic neurons are in sacral segments (S2-S4), not thoracic lamina II.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in lateral horn (lamina VII, T1-L2/3)

questions.text: The main sensory nucleus of spinal cord is:
questions.explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
questions.keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn

questions.text: Which of the following tracts DON'T extend to all segment of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract is present only in upper cervical segments (C1-C6/8), originating from the tectum of midbrain. It does not extend to all spinal cord levels, unlike the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract does NOT extend to all spinal segments (present only in upper cervical)

questions.text: Which of the following tracts lie in the dorsal funiculus?
questions.explanation: The dorsal (posterior) funiculus contains the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus. The rubrospinal tract is in the lateral funiculus; vestibulospinal tract is in the ventral funiculus.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract (fasciculus cuneatus) lies in the dorsal funiculus

questions.text: Which of the following tracts is present in all segments of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract is present in all spinal cord segments, carrying proprioceptive information from lower limbs to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract present in all spinal cord segments
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.

questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: The first-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body has its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (spinal ganglion). Its central process enters the spinal cord and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: First-order proprioception neuron cell body in dorsal root ganglion

questions.text: The second order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.

questions.text: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in:
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) relay to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. They carry information that has already decussated at the level of the inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the inferior olivary nucleus
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.

questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline) in the medulla, and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. They are the second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei, form medial lemniscus
options: Arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Terminate at gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Carry proprioceptive impulses from the head.

questions.text: One of the following is true about gracile tract:
questions.explanation: The gracile tract (fasciculus gracilis) carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower half of the body, is present in ALL levels of the spinal cord (not just cervical/thoracic), and terminates at the gracile nucleus in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract: present in ALL levels, carries lower body proprioception to gracile nucleus
options: Presents only in cervical & thoracic levels of spinal cord.
Carries proprioception from the upper half of the body.
Terminates at gracile nucleus in medulla.
Arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.

questions.text: One of the following is true about cuneate tract:
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of the upper half of the body (above T6), enters the spinal cord, and ascends without crossing to terminate at the cuneate nucleus. The cuneate nucleus is ipsilateral.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of upper body, ipsilateral cuneate nucleus
options: It arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on same side.
It arises from cuneate nucleus on opposite side.
It is present in lateral column of white matter in spinal cord.

questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium (ependymal)
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.text: Which of the following cells produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). In the PNS, Schwann cells produce myelin. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages to clear debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.text: Endothelial cells of blood capillaries in brain characterized by having:
questions.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles (not more), abundant mitochondria (for transport functions), tight junctions (not few), and few desmosomes. Tight junctions are essential for the blood-brain barrier function.
questions.keyConcept: Brain endothelium: tight junctions, few pinocytic vesicles (blood-brain barrier)

questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
questions.keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers are NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic) - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in:
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
questions.keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)

questions.text: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) that form a delicate connective tissue layer closely applied to the brain surface. It contains blood vessels that penetrate the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal origin)

questions.text: Tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the blood-CSF barrier, preventing free diffusion between blood and CSF. The blood-brain barrier is formed by astrocyte foot processes and tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier (not blood-brain)
