More convergence of afferent nerve fibers

questions.text: Which stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) respond to noxious stimuli including intense mechanical distortion, heat (>45C), and chemical irritants (bradykinin, substance P, prostaglandins).
questions.keyConcept: Nociceptors are polymodal free nerve endings responding to mechanical, thermal, and chemical noxious stimuli.

questions.text: Which statement regarding sensory fiber conduction is correct?
questions.explanation: Sensory fiber conduction velocity correlates with fiber diameter: A-delta fibers (5-15 m/s) transmit fast pain; C fibers (0.5-2 m/s) transmit slow pain. Myelination increases conduction velocity.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction velocity in sensory fibers depends on diameter and myelination: A-delta > C fibers.
options: Crude touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Fine touch is carried on C fibers
Fine touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Vibration sense is carried on Aδ fibers
Nociceptive stimuli are carried on Aβ fibers

questions.text: Which type of pain is transmitted by Aδ nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers transmit fast, sharp, well-localized pain (first pain) via the neospinothalamic tract. C fibers transmit slow, dull, poorly localized pain (second pain) via the paleospinothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers mediate fast, localized pain; C fibers mediate slow, diffuse pain.

questions.text: Sudden increase in skin temperature above 50 °C leads to:
questions.explanation: Heat above 50C stimulates thermal nociceptors (via TRPV1 channels) causing burning pain. Temperatures above 45C begin to activate pain receptors, with noxious heat stimulating C and A-delta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: TRPV1 receptors on nociceptors respond to temperatures above 43-45C, triggering burning pain sensation.
options: Transient impulses due to damage of cold receptors above 40 °C

questions.text: Which fibers transmit crude touch sensation?
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by A-beta fibers via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway (fasciculus cuneatus for upper body, fasciculus gracilis for lower body). Fine touch uses the same pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch travels via dorsal column pathways (A-beta fibers) to the thalamus and sensory cortex.

questions.text: Which substance stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Bradykinin, substance P, histamine, prostaglandins, and serotonin are all algogenic substances that stimulate nociceptors and cause pain when released during tissue injury or inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Algogenic substances (bradykinin, prostaglandins, substance P) sensitize and activate nociceptors.

questions.text: Which nerve fibers transmit warm temperature sensation?
questions.explanation: Warm temperature sensation (30-45C) is transmitted by C fibers via the lateral spinothalamic tract to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamic nucleus, then to sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Warm receptors are C fiber thermoreceptors projecting via spinothalamic tract to VPL thalamus.

questions.text: Fast pain is characterized by which duration?
questions.explanation: Fast pain (A-delta fibers) has a duration of approximately 0.1 seconds, occurring immediately after stimulus and enabling rapid localization of noxious stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is brief (~0.1s) and well-localized due to A-delta fiber conduction.

questions.text: Which clinical sign is seen in chronic gastritis due to inflammation of the stomach wall?
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis causing inflammation of the stomach body (where parietal cells are located) leads to loss of intrinsic factor and reduced acid production, resulting in pernicious anemia with neurological manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal cell destruction in body gastritis causes intrinsic factor deficiency and pernicious anemia.

questions.text: In secondary hyperalgesia, which describes the affected area?
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperalgesia occurs in the surrounding undamaged tissue adjacent to the primary injury site, where nociceptors become sensitized by inflammatory mediators released from damaged cells.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary hyperalgesia extends beyond the injury site due to central sensitization of dorsal horn neurons.
options: Inflamed tissue directly exposed to noxious stimuli
All dermatomes sharing the same dorsal root ganglion

questions.text: Which explains pain relief when you rub the skin near an injury?
questions.explanation: Rubbing the skin activates A-beta mechanoreceptors that inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn through gating mechanisms in the substantia gelatinosa (gate control theory).
questions.keyConcept: Gate control theory: tactile stimulation inhibits nociceptive transmission via A-beta fiber activation of inhibitory interneurons in dorsal horn.

questions.text: A woman wore a dress on the beach. Later, wearing a jacket over the same area caused pain. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Wearing a jacket over tanned skin causes referred pain from sunburned skin, demonstrating referred pain where visceral or deep somatic injury is perceived as cutaneous pain.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain from deep tissue injury can be perceived as cutaneous pain due to convergence of somatic and visceral afferents on dorsal horn neurons.
options: Increase receptor sensitivity by tissue products
Activity-dependent increase in excitability of dorsal horn neurons
Increased threshold of peripheral nociceptors due to inflammatory mediators
Decreased inhibitory interneuron function in the spinal cord
Impaired saltatory conduction in primary afferent neurons

questions.text: Which receptors inhibit pain sensation in the CNS?
questions.explanation: Endogenous opioid peptides (endorphins and enkephalins) released from periaqueductal gray and nucleus raphe magnus inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
questions.keyConcept: Endogenous opioid peptides from brainstem nuclei inhibit nociceptive transmission in the spinal cord dorsal horn.

questions.text: Extracranial headache is an example of:
questions.explanation: Extracranial headache originates from structures outside the cranium such as muscles, vessels, or nerves in the scalp and face (e.g., tension headache, cluster headache).
questions.keyConcept: Extracranial headaches arise from pericranial structures; intracranial headaches involve meninges or blood vessels.

questions.text: Acupuncture relieves pain mainly by:
questions.explanation: Acupuncture relieves pain primarily by stimulating A-beta fibers that activate descending inhibitory pathways from PAG to nucleus raphe magnus, releasing endogenous opioids.
questions.keyConcept: Acupuncture activates descending inhibitory pathways via A-beta fiber stimulation and endogenous opioid release.
options: Gate control theory and psychogenic excitation
Blockade of sodium channels in sensory nerves

questions.text: Deep pain is typically characterized by:
questions.explanation: Deep pain (visceral or deep somatic) is poorly localized, often aching or cramping, and may be referred to distant dermatomes. It is transmitted by C fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pain is dull, poorly localized, and may be referred due to convergence of deep and superficial afferents.
options: Rapidly conducted by Aδ fibers only

questions.text: Referred pain from the gallbladder is most commonly felt in which area?
questions.explanation: Gallbladder pain is commonly referred to the right scapular region (C3-C5 dermatomes) due to shared central pathways with phrenic nerve dermatomes.
questions.keyConcept: Gallbladder referred pain typically localizes to the right shoulder/scapular area via C3-C5 pathways.

questions.text: Which is a cause of extracranial headache?
questions.explanation: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction is a cause of extracranial headache. Intracranial causes include meningitis, tumor, or vascular events.
questions.keyConcept: TMJ dysfunction and muscle tension are common extracranial headache causes originating from pericranial structures.

questions.text: The initial phase of a migraine attack is associated with which vascular event?
questions.explanation: The initial phase of migraine involves cortical spreading depression followed by vasoconstriction causing the aura. Later phases involve vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Migraine starts with cortical spreading depression and vasoconstriction (aura), followed by vasodilation causing headache.

questions.text: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of form and texture) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway for fine touch and proprioception to reach the sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioception for object recognition.

questions.text: Which statement is true regarding deep pressure sensation?
questions.explanation: Deep pressure sensation is transmitted by A-beta fibers via dorsal column pathways and by A-delta fibers via spinothalamic tracts. It has a high threshold compared to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pressure uses A-beta fibers in dorsal columns and A-delta fibers in spinothalamic tracts.
options: It is mediated by slowly adapting receptors
It is transmitted only by free nerve endings
It adapts rapidly to sustained stimulus
It is carried exclusively by Aδ fibers
It is not associated with vibration

questions.text: Which statement is correct regarding muscle tone?
questions.explanation: Muscle tone is maintained by tonic stretch reflex activity mediated by muscle spindles and gamma motor neurons. It reflects baseline contraction maintaining posture.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle tone results from tonic gamma motor neuron activity maintaining muscle spindle sensitivity.
options: It depends only on upper motor neurons
It is absent during normal posture
It is mediated by polysynaptic reflex

questions.text: Which statement regarding muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ is correct?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles detect length changes and initiate stretch reflexes; Golgi tendon organs detect tension changes and provide protective inhibition. Both contribute to proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles respond to length; Golgi tendon organs respond to tension for reflexive motor control.
options: Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tension
Golgi tendon organ initiates the stretch reflex
Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tone
Golgi tendon organ has damping function
Muscle spindle is located in the tendon

questions.text: Facilitation of stretch reflex is done by:
questions.explanation: Facilitation of stretch reflex is achieved by gamma motor neurons that contract intrafusal fibers, increasing spindle sensitivity and reflex excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons facilitate stretch reflex by contracting intrafusal fibers and enhancing spindle discharge.

questions.text: Which pair correctly matches a reflex with its sensory receptor?
questions.explanation: The inverse stretch reflex (autogenic inhibition) uses Golgi tendon organs as receptors that inhibit alpha motor neurons when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organs mediate inverse stretch reflex to prevent muscle damage from excessive tension.

questions.text: Oscillating, interrupted voluntary movements typically occur due to loss of which function?
questions.explanation: Loss of cerebellar function causes decomposition of movement and dysmetria. Oscillating interrupted movements (intention tremor) occur due to loss of coordination and timing.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions cause intention tremor from loss of coordination and timing of voluntary movements.

questions.text: The Golgi tendon organ provides input to which neurons?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs synapse on Ib inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that inhibit alpha motor neurons of the homonymous muscle, providing protective autogenic inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organs activate Ib inhibitory interneurons to autogenically inhibit muscle contraction under high tension.

questions.text: A patient presents with hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes, and signs of an UMN lesion. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: An UMN lesion causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and loss of superficial reflexes. The clasp-knife response is a characteristic feature.
questions.keyConcept: UMN syndrome includes spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and loss of superficial reflexes with clasp-knife response.

questions.text: Which function is attributed to the pontine circuit in motor control?
questions.explanation: Pontine reticulospinal tracts facilitate extensor tone and antigravity muscles, important for posture and righting reflexes. They are part of the medial descending systems.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine reticulospinal tract facilitates extensor muscles for postural control and righting.
options: Storage of plan of skilled movement

questions.text: Ankle clonus occurs due to:
questions.explanation: Ankle clonus results from hyperactive stretch reflexes where sustained muscle stretch produces rhythmic oscillating contractions due to UMN lesions and increased gamma motor neuron activity.
questions.keyConcept: Clonus is a sustained stretch reflex response from hyperexcitable muscle spindles in UMN lesions.

questions.text: Which pattern of sensory loss is characteristic of peripheral neuritis?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuritis causes stocking-glove sensory loss (distal symmetric loss) affecting all sensory modalities due to length-dependent axonal degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Peripheral neuritis produces symmetric distal sensory loss in stocking-glove distribution from length-dependent neuropathy.

questions.text: Which accurately describes the pattern of dissociative sensory loss in syringomyelia?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss with loss of pain and temperature but preserved touch and proprioception due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central canal.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia selectively damages crossing spinothalamic fibers, causing cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function.
options: Loss of pain and touch with preservation of temperature
Loss of touch and temperature with preservation of pain
Loss of pain with preservation of touch and temperature
Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch
Loss of temperature with preservation of touch and pain

questions.text: In syringomyelia, sensory loss typically follows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia cord lesion pattern

questions.text: Which brain structure is typically damaged in left‑sided hemiballismus?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus results from damage to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, causing violent flinging movements of the opposite side of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Subthalamic nucleus lesions

questions.text: Glutamate is secreted by:
questions.explanation: Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.
questions.keyConcept: Corticostriatal projection

questions.text: Which statement about climbing fibers is correct?
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers originate from the inferior olivary nucleus, form powerful excitatory synapses on Purkinje cells, each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber, and they play a role in motor learning.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fiber characteristics
options: They originate from the inferior olivary nucleus
They form powerful excitatory synapses on Purkinje cells
Each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber
They play a role in motor learning

questions.text: Tremors present during voluntary movement and reduced during sleep indicate which condition?
questions.explanation: Intention tremor (present during voluntary movement, reduced during sleep) is characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction, as opposed to resting tremor seen in basal ganglia disorders.
questions.keyConcept: Intention tremor characteristics

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the gate control theory of pain?
questions.explanation: The gate control theory proposes that large myelinated afferent fibers (touch) can inhibit transmission of pain signals in the dorsal horn through interneurons, effectively 'closing the gate' on pain perception.
questions.keyConcept: Gate control: large afferent fiber activity inhibits dorsal horn pain transmission.
options: Pain is transmitted only by large myelinated fibres.
Activity in large afferent fibres can inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
Pain is solely a cortical phenomenon.
Endorphins are released only from the pituitary.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (-70mV) most closely matches K+ equilibrium potential (-90mV) because the membrane is more permeable to K+ at rest through leak channels.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential closest to K+ equilibrium potential.

questions.text:
The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory A 1:
A. Crude Touch.
B. Fast pain.
C. Vibration sense.
D. Proprioceptive sensation.
E. Stereognosis.
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by the anterior spinothalamic tract, not by somatosensory area 1 which processes fine/discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 does not process crude touch (anterior spinothalamic does).

questions.text:
If the gamma efferent discharge to a muscle is sectioned, what you expect to happen:
A. The muscle will be paralyzed.
B. Increased muscle spindle sensitivity
C. Energy consumption by brain is the same.
D. Ability to carry a load is affected.
E. Tone of the muscle is not affected.
questions.explanation: Sectioning gamma efferents reduces spindle sensitivity, impairing load detection and the ability to make automatic adjustments during weight-bearing activities.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma efferent sectioning: reduced load-carrying ability due to loss of spindle sensitivity.
options: Energy consumption by brain is the same
Ability to carry a load is affected
Tone of the muscle is not affected

questions.text:
When you passively and slowly stretch a muscle, which of the following afferent fiber will continue to discharge:
A. Ia neurons
B. II neurons
C. Ib neurons
D. IIa neurons
E. Y neurons
questions.explanation: Type II (secondary) afferents from nuclear bag and chain fibers in muscle spindles continue firing during slow sustained stretch, unlike rapidly adapting Ia fibers which fire only during changes.
questions.keyConcept: Type II (secondary) afferents fire during slow sustained stretch (non-adapting).

questions.text:
The withdrawal reflex is initiated by stimulation of which of the following receptors?
A. Muscle spindle
B. Joint capsule receptor
C. Cutaneous free nerve ending
D. Golgi tendon organ
E. Pacinian corpuscles
questions.explanation: The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is initiated by cutaneous nociceptors (free nerve endings) detecting painful stimuli, activating flexor muscles to remove the limb from the harmful stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Withdrawal reflex initiated by cutaneous free nerve endings (nociceptors).

questions.text:
An athlete was carrying a heavy weight during a competition for a time and then he suddenly left it. This could be explained by activation of:
A. IIb fibers
B. Ia fibers
C. Ib fibers
D. Gamma efferent fibers
E. a motor neurons
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (Ib fibers) detect muscle tension; when tension becomes excessive, they trigger autogenic inhibition to protect the muscle from damage by relaxing it.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organ (Ib fibers): autogenic inhibition when tension excessive.

questions.text:
Reflex contraction of the extensor muscles of the right leg can occur following:
A. Hitting a chair with the left foot.
B. Stretching the flexor muscles in the right leg
C. Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand
D. Excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg
E. Painful kicking of the right knee.
questions.explanation: The crossed extensor reflex causes the contralateral extensor to contract when a limb is withdrawn from pain, allowing weight shift and postural support while the affected side flexes.
questions.keyConcept: Crossed extensor reflex: contralateral extensor contraction when ipsilateral limb withdrawn from pain.
options: Hitting a chair with the left foot
Stretching the flexor muscles in the right leg
Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand
Excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg
Painful kicking of the right knee

questions.text:
A patient has lesion in right motor area 4, he will have:
A. Loss fine discrete movements in right leg
B. Loss of fine discrete movements in left hand
C. Complete loss of gross movements in right hand
D. Increased muscle tone in right leg
E. Decreased muscle tone in right hand.
questions.explanation: A lesion in the right motor area 4 causes loss of fine discrete movements in the contralateral (left) hand due to the crossed corticospinal tract; this is classic upper motor neuron weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Right motor cortex lesion: loss of fine movements in left hand (contralateral).
options: Loss fine discrete movements in right leg
Loss of fine discrete movements in left hand
Complete loss of gross movements in right hand
Increased muscle tone in right leg
Decreased muscle tone in right hand

questions.text:
A high school student was trying to solve a math problem. Which of the following is the expected brain EEG waves in this case?
A. Alpha waves
B. Beta waves
C. Theta waves
D. Delta waves
E. Gamma waves
questions.explanation: Gamma waves (30-100 Hz) are associated with high-level cognitive processing and appear during complex problem-solving tasks requiring focused attention.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma waves: present during active problem-solving and cognitive tasks.

questions.text:
A wife came to the doctor, and complained that her husband talks during his sleep, and that frightens her, the doctor explained that:
A. This is normal in REM sleep
B. She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
C. Teeth grinding is expected to happen
D. She can easily wake him up
E. This probably happens a lot near the morning
questions.explanation: Sleep talking occurs during REM sleep when motor inhibition prevents dream enactment, but the person is difficult to wake from this stage; they typically won't remember the dream.
questions.keyConcept: Sleep talking occurs in REM; difficult to wake, no dream recall.
options: This is normal in REM sleep
She can ask her husband about his dream, and he will probably remember them
Teeth grinding is expected to happen
She can easily wake him up
This probably happens a lot near the morning

questions.text:
The memory of a sequence of events in which a person participated is called:
A. Semantic memory
B. Episodic
C. Implicit
D. Procedural
E. Conditional
questions.explanation: Episodic memory records personal experiences organized in time sequence (autobiographical memory), allowing recall of events in which one actively participated.
questions.keyConcept: Episodic memory: memory of personal events in sequence.

questions.text:
Semantic memory is characterized by which of the following?
A. It is the memory of personal events
B. A type of implicit memory
C. It is the memory of facts
D. It is non-declarative memory
E. It is a procedural memory
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is explicit/declarative memory for facts and knowledge about the world (general facts), distinct from episodic memory (personal events) and procedural memory (skills).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory: memory of facts (general knowledge).
options: It is the memory of personal events
It is the memory of facts

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists
questions.explanation: Insomnia is NOT an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists. Option C is correct. D2 agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) commonly cause hallucinations, dyskinesia (especially with long-term use), and impulse control disorders. Insomnia is not a typical adverse effect; actually, these drugs can cause daytime sleepiness. Amantadine is known to cause insomnia.
questions.keyConcept: D2 agonists cause neuropsychiatric effects (hallucinations, dyskinesia, impulse control disorders) but not insomnia.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of amantadine
questions.explanation: Daytime sleepiness is NOT an adverse effect of amantadine. Option B is correct. Amantadine causes hallucinations, livedo reticularis (skin rash), ankle edema, and tolerance. Insomnia is actually a known amantadine effect (along with dizziness). Daytime sleepiness is more typical of dopamine agonists.
questions.keyConcept: Amantadine commonly causes insomnia, livedo reticularis, and ankle edema, but not daytime sleepiness.

questions.text: Addition of the following drugs to L dopa produce all the following except
questions.explanation: Entacapone DECREASES L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Entacapone inhibits COMT, which DECREASES L-dopa metabolism, thereby INCREASING its bioavailability and duration of action. Domperidone decreases nausea (A is correct). Benztropine decreases absorption (B is correct). Apomorphine decreases off time (C is correct).
questions.keyConcept: COMT inhibitors like entacapone prolong L-dopa action by preventing its peripheral breakdown.
options: Domperidone / decreases l dopa induced nausea & vomiting
Apomorphine / decreases off time of on-off phenomena
Entacapone / Decrease L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action

questions.text: Cross match
questions.explanation: This matching question requires pairing drug names with their adverse effects. Amantadine causes insomnia, livedo reticularis, and ankle edema. Entacapone causes orange discoloration of urine and diarrhea. Bromocriptine causes vasospasm and cardiac fibrosis. Selegiline causes insomnia and hallucination. Pramipexole causes daytime sleepiness and impulse control disorders. Benztropine causes dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention (anticholinergic effects).
questions.keyConcept: Antiparkinsonian drugs have distinct adverse effect profiles important for clinical management and drug selection.

pairs.target: Day time sleepiness & impulse control disorders

questions.text: Addition of carbidopa to L dopa increases risk of all the following adverse effects except
questions.explanation: Nausea & vomiting is NOT increased by adding carbidopa. Option C is correct. Carbidopa prevents peripheral conversion of L-dopa to dopamine, reducing peripheral side effects including nausea/vomiting. However, it increases brain dopamine, which can increase CNS adverse effects: dyskinesia, hallucinations, and confusion.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa reduces peripheral L-dopa side effects (nausea) but increases central dopaminergic effects (dyskinesia, hallucinations).

questions.text: Conscious sedation may be induced by
questions.explanation: Fentanyl with Midazolam induces conscious sedation. Option A is correct. This combination (opioid + benzodiazepine) provides analgesia and amnesia for conscious sedation in minor procedures. Droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia (B). Domperidone is antiemetic (C).
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation combines fentanyl (analgesia) with midazolam (anxiolysis/amnesia) for procedural sedation.

questions.text: The following is not correctly matched to its use:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is not used for panic attack - this is NOT correctly matched. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is used for generalized anxiety, not panic attacks (which require benzodiazepines or SSRIs). Diazepam for muscle spasticity (A correct). Midazolam for anesthesia (B correct). Clonazepam for epilepsy (C correct).
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a selective anxiolytic for generalized anxiety but lacks efficacy for panic attacks.

questions.text: The following concerning zolpidem is not true
questions.explanation: Zolpidem is LESS liable to induce rebound insomnia than benzodiazepines - this is NOT true. Option C is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has more rebound insomnia potential compared to benzodiazepines because of its short half-life and selective BZ1 receptor action. Options A, B, D are true: zolpidem is short-acting with less hangover, acts on BZ1 receptor, and has less tolerance/dependence than BZDs.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has a short half-life and less hangover than benzodiazepines, but can cause rebound insomnia due to its short duration of action.
options: It is a short acting hypnotic causing less hang over than benzodiazepines
More liable to induce rebound insomnia & disturbance in REM sleep than benzodiazepines.
Its use is associated with less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines.

questions.text: The major limitation to the use of benzodiazepines in anxiety is:
questions.explanation: Dependence is the major limitation to benzodiazepine use. Option C is correct. Benzodiazepines cause physical and psychological dependence with chronic use, limiting their long-term use. Options A, B, D are less accurate: flumazenil is an antidote (A is wrong), cardiovascular depression is rare (B), and respiratory depression is mainly with high doses or combined with other depressants (D).
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dependence is the primary clinical limitation, requiring careful prescribing and monitoring.
options: No antidote is available if overdose toxicity occurs.

questions.text: An anxiolytic useful in a patient with a history of drug dependence is:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is preferred in patients with drug dependence history. Option A is correct. Buspirone has no abuse potential, no physical dependence, and can be used safely in patients with history of substance abuse. All other benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, lorazepam) have dependence liability.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's lack of dependence makes it safe for patients with substance abuse history.

questions.text: The dose of benzodiazepines should be adjusted in:
questions.explanation: Dose adjustment is needed in elderly AND with alcohol AND with hepatic dysfunction. Option D is correct. All three factors require dose adjustment: elderly have reduced metabolism, alcohol potentiates CNS depression, hepatic dysfunction impairs metabolism of benzodiazepines.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dosing requires adjustment in elderly, hepatic impairment, and when combined with CNS depressants.

questions.text: The following concerning the use of benzodiazepines is not true
questions.explanation: Shorter acting agents are NOT preferred as anxiolytics - this is NOT true. Option D is incorrect. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) are preferred for anxiety because they provide steady plasma levels. Short-acting agents (triazolam) cause more rebound anxiety and are used for insomnia. Options A, B, C are correct: abuse causes memory loss, toxic dose causes prolonged sleep, flumazenil reverses respiratory depression.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred for anxiety due to stable plasma concentrations and reduced rebound effects.
options: Abuse is associated with memory loss.
Toxic dose results in prolonged sleep.
Respiratory depression is reversed by flumazenil.
Shorter acting agents are preferred as anxiolytics.

questions.text: A drug whose toxic dose results in prolonged sleep reversed by flumazenil
questions.explanation: Triazolam toxic dose results in prolonged sleep reversed by flumazenil. Option C is correct. Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine; overdose causes prolonged sedation reversed by flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist). Pentobarbital and phenobarbital are barbiturates (not reversed by flumazenil). Buspirone is not a sedative.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine overdose but not barbiturate overdose.

questions.text: Flumazenil is an antidote for all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is NOT reversed by flumazenil. Option B is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. Triazolam (A), zolpidem (C), and diazepam (D) are all benzodiazepine-related drugs reversed by flumazenil. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A agonist anxiolytic that does not act on benzodiazepine receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil only reverses benzodiazepines and zolpidem; it does not reverse buspirone (5-HT1A agonist) or barbiturates.

questions.text: All the following characteristics are shared by flumazenil and naloxone Except:
questions.explanation: Flumazenil and naloxone are NOT given orally - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Both flumazenil and naloxone are given parenterally (IV), not orally, because they have poor oral bioavailability and rapid first-pass metabolism. Options A, C, D are correct shared characteristics.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil and naloxone require parenteral administration due to poor oral bioavailability and rapid hepatic metabolism.
options: Have shorter t1/2 than their respective agonists.
Given in anesthesia to reverse CNS depression of their agonists.
Specific respiratory stimulants in benzodiazepine or opioid toxicity.

questions.text: Abuse potential of buspirone is low because
questions.explanation: Buspirone has delayed onset of action - this explains low abuse potential. Option C is correct. Unlike benzodiazepines which act immediately, buspirone takes 2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect. This delayed onset, combined with lack of sedation and no GABA activity, results in low abuse potential.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's delayed onset of action contributes to its minimal abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines.
options: It has a weak anxiolytic effect
It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters.
It has a delayed onset of action.
Its marked sedating effect is troublesome.

questions.text: The following anxiolytic drug do not act through GABA
questions.explanation: Buspirone does not act through GABA. Option B is correct. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist anxiolytic. Zolpidem (A), lorazepam (C), and phenobarbital (D) all enhance GABAergic transmission. Buspirone works through serotonin modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A serotonin receptor partial agonist, distinct from GABA-acting anxiolytics.

questions.text: The following drug has no sedative hypnotic effect
questions.explanation: Flumazenil has no sedative hypnotic effect. Option C is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that blocks GABA-benzodiazepine receptors. It reverses sedation and would not cause sedation. Antihistamines (A), tricyclics (B), and clonidine (D) all have sedative effects.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with no intrinsic sedative activity.

questions.text: The following drug is not matched with its mechanism of action
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5HT1A AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is a selective 5-HT1A partial agonist (not antagonist). Options A, B, C are correct: diazepam increases frequency of chloride channel opening, zolpidem binds BZ1 receptor, barbiturates increase duration of channel opening.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's anxiolytic effect comes from 5-HT1A receptor partial agonism, not antagonism.
options: Diazepam increases frequency of opening of chloride channels
Zolpidem binds with BZD1 subtype → increases GABA activity
Barbiturates increase duration of opening of chloride channels

questions.text: The following is a Wrong statement about Barbiturates
questions.explanation: Barbiturates are NOT strong enzyme inducers - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Barbiturates are potent CYP450 inducers, increasing metabolism of many drugs. Options A, C, D are correct: low therapeutic index, dose-dependent CNS depression, no specific antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates are potent enzyme inducers that increase hepatic metabolism of many co-administered drugs.
options: Dose dependent CNS depression up to coma

questions.text: The following statement is Wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of Benzodiazepines
questions.explanation: Clinical duration of long-acting BZDs is longer than actual half-life - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Long-acting BZDs form active metabolites that prolong their effect beyond the parent compound's half-life. Options A, B, D are correct: IM absorption is slower (except lorazepam), lorazepam uses glucuronidation not oxidation, lorazepam has no active metabolites.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines have prolonged effects due to active metabolites, making actual duration longer than parent half-life.
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BDZs is shorter than the actual half life as they form active metabolites

questions.text: BDZs do not induce the following effect
questions.explanation: BDZs do NOT decrease stage II NREM sleep. Option B is correct. Benzodiazepines decrease REM sleep and stages III/IV (deep sleep), but actually increase stage II NREM sleep (light sleep). This is why they suppress deep sleep and REM sleep while promoting light sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines suppress REM and deep sleep (III/IV) while preserving or increasing light sleep (stage II).
options: Decrease stage II of NREM sleep
Decrease stage III & IV of NREM sleep

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of BZDS
questions.explanation: Decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal is NOT an adverse effect - it is a withdrawal effect. Option B is incorrect. Insomnia and REM rebound occur on withdrawal, not as direct adverse effects during use. Options A, C, D are correct direct adverse effects: sedation/hangover, cognitive impairment, tolerance/dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine withdrawal causes REM rebound insomnia; direct adverse effects include sedation, cognitive impairment, and dependence.
options: Insomnia & decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal
Decrease in cognitive function of the brain

questions.text: The following is a Wrong statement about BZDs
questions.explanation: Midazolam is NOT long acting - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used in anesthesia. Lorazepam is intermediate-acting (correct A). Alprazolam is effective for panic (correct C). Diazepam is long-acting for alcohol withdrawal (correct D).
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for induction of anesthesia and procedural sedation.
options: Lorazepam is an intermediate duration and effective anxiolytic and in status epilepticus
Midazolam is long acting acting used in anesthesia as hypnotic and should be avoided as anxiolytic
Alprazolam is effective in controlling the panic attacks
Diazepam is long acting & useful during alcohol withdrwal

questions.text: The following is wrong about zolpidem
questions.explanation: Tolerance and dependence is LESS common with zolpidem than BZDs - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has LESS dependence potential than benzodiazepines. Options A, B, C are correct: zolpidem is short-acting non-BZD, has less hangover/rebound, and toxicity is reversed by flumazenil.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has lower dependence potential than benzodiazepines despite being a GABA-A receptor modulator.
options: Less hangover and rebound insomnia than BDZ
Its toxicity can be reversed by flumazenil
Tolerance & dependence is more common than BDZs

questions.text: Choose the Incorrect statement
questions.explanation: Ramelteon is a melatonin RECEPTOR AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Ramelteon is a selective melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist used for insomnia. Options A, C, D are correct: buspirone is selective anxiolytic, flumazenil is BZD antagonist, eszopiclone is non-BZD hypnotic.
questions.keyConcept: Ramelteon works as a melatonin receptor agonist, not antagonist, to promote sleep.
options: Buspirone is selective anxiolytic with delayed onset of action
Ramelteon is selective melatonin receptors antagonist
Flumazenil is short acting BDZ receptor antagonist
Eszopiclone is intermediate acting non BDZ hypnotic

questions.text: The following statement is wrong
questions.explanation: Panic disorders do NOT require highly potent drugs such as alprazolam AND buspirone - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Alprazolam is highly potent and effective for panic; buspirone is NOT effective for acute panic attacks. SSRIs are first-line for panic disorder. Option E about hepatic impairment is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Panic disorder is treated with SSRIs or high-potency benzodiazepines (alprazolam); buspirone is ineffective for panic.
options: Chronic anxiety is added to antidepressant in the beginning of therapy till the effect of antidepressant appears
Chronic insomnia should be treatment with antidepressant such as mirtazapine
Short acting BDZs are preferred in insomnia with difficulty in falling asleep
Panic disorders require highly potent drugs such as alprazolam & buspirone
Dose adjustment for most of BDZs is required in hepatic impairment

questions.text: The following about thiopental is WRONG:
questions.explanation: Thiopental is NOT ultra-short acting due to rapid metabolism - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Thiopental is ultra-short acting due to RAPID DISTRIBUTION out of the brain, not rapid metabolism. It undergoes slow hepatic metabolism but rapid redistribution causes short duration. Options A, C, D are correct: rapid onset, enzyme inducer, no antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Thiopental's ultra-short duration is due to rapid redistribution from brain to other tissues, not rapid metabolism.
options: Has a rapid onset of action due to rapid crossing of BBB.
Ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Enzyme inducer and may precipitate porphyria.
May induce respiratory depression with no available antidote.

questions.text: A drug inducing a GABA- mediated sedative hypnotic effect in intensive care units
questions.explanation: Propofol induces GABA-mediated sedation in ICU. Option B is correct. Propofol enhances GABA-A receptor activity, providing sedation. Ketamine (C) acts on NMDA receptors. Fentanyl (A) is opioid. Propofol is preferred for ICU sedation due to rapid onset/offset and easy titration.
questions.keyConcept: Propofol provides GABAergic sedation with rapid onset and recovery, ideal for ICU sedation protocols.

questions.text: Dentists avoid extraction in infection because of all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Infection INCREASES extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics - this is FALSE. Option D is incorrect. Infection lowers pH (acidic), which DECREASES the unionized (active) form of local anesthetics (which are weak bases). The unionized form crosses nerve membranes; acidic conditions trap the drug in ionized form extracellularly. Options A, B, C are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Infection's acidic environment reduces local anesthetic efficacy by decreasing the unionized (nerve-penetrating) form.
options: Infection decreases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.
Infection reduces crossing of local anesthetics inside nerve cell.
Infection increases extracellular unionized form of local anesthetics.

questions.text: The following is not true about cocaine:
questions.explanation: Cocaine is a potent VASOCONSTRICTOR, not vasodilator. Option C is incorrect. Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake, causing vasoconstriction and hypertension. This is why it causes local anesthesia without needing epinephrine. Options A, B, D are correct: cocaine is a local anesthetic, can cause convulsions, and chronic use causes psychosis.
questions.keyConcept: Cocaine's vasoconstrictor properties (from norepinephrine reuptake inhibition) distinguish it from other local anesthetics.
options: Acute toxicity may result in convulsions.

questions.text: The following is not adverse effect of halothane
questions.explanation: Halothane causes hypotension, not hypertension. Option C is incorrect. Halothane causes cardiovascular depression: bradycardia, hypotension, and arrhythmias. It also causes malignant hyperthermia, hepatic toxicity, and increases ICP. The vasodilation and myocardial depression lead to hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Halothane's cardiovascular effects include bradycardia, hypotension, and arrhythmias due to myocardial depression.

questions.text: Nitrous oxide, the following is incorrect
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide does NOT cause iron deficiency anemia - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Nitrous oxide inactivates vitamin B12, causing megaloblastic anemia (not iron deficiency). Options A, B, C are correct: N2O is weak analgesic, safer than halothane, and causes abuse with prolonged exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide causes B12 inactivation and megaloblastic anemia with chronic use, not iron deficiency.
options: Safer than halothane with less respiratory depression and less hepatic toxicity
Risk of abuse on prolonged exposure
Iron deficiency anemia on chronic exposure

questions.text: The following is not common adverse effect of nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Hepatic toxicity is NOT a common adverse effect of nitrous oxide. Option D is correct. N2O is minimally metabolized and has excellent safety profile. Hypoxia (A), middle ear pressure (B), and abortion risk (C) are documented concerns. Unlike halothane, N2O rarely causes hepatotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide has minimal hepatic toxicity unlike halogenated anesthetics.
options: Hypoxia if take pure without oxygen
Increase pressure in the middle ear

questions.text: Which of the following is wrong regarding propofol?
questions.explanation: Respiratory depression and vomiting are NOT common adverse effects of propofol - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Propofol commonly causes respiratory depression AND vomiting. Options A, B, D are correct: rapid induction/recovery, used in sedation, suitable for day surgery.
questions.keyConcept: Propofol commonly causes respiratory depression and nausea, requiring careful monitoring during administration.
options: Rapid induction & rapid recovery due to rapid metabolism
Used in conscious and deep sedation
Respiratory depression and vomiting are common adverse effect
Useful in one day surgery as intravenous anesthetic

questions.text: Which of the following is wrong regarding ketamine?
questions.explanation: Ketamine INCREASES blood pressure, not decreases - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Ketamine stimulates sympathetic nervous system, causing hypertension and tachycardia. Options A, B, D are correct: short-acting IV dissociative anesthetic, profound analgesia, hallucinations on recovery.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects cause hypertension and tachycardia, not hypotension.
options: Short acting IV agent producing dissociative anesthesia
Useful in hypertension as it decrease blood pressure

questions.text: Which of the following is not adverse effect of spinal anesthesia
questions.explanation: Hypertension is NOT an adverse effect of spinal anesthesia. Option D is correct. Spinal anesthesia causes hypotension (not hypertension) due to sympathetic block and vasodilation. Options A, B, C are recognized complications: post-dural puncture headache, nerve root irritation, meningitis.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal anesthesia causes hypotension due to sympathetic blockade, not hypertension.

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
questions.explanation: Felypressin IS suitable with local anesthetics in cardiac patients - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Felypressin (vasopressin analog) is preferred over epinephrine in cardiac patients because it has less cardiac effects. Option A, B, C are correct: propranolol decreases lidocaine metabolism, epinephrine with alpha unopposed action causes hypertension, TCA/MAOI combo with epinephrine risks hypertensive crisis.
questions.keyConcept: Felypressin is the vasoconstrictor of choice in cardiac patients due to minimal cardiac stimulation.
options: Propranolol decrease metabolism of lidocaine and may precipitate its toxicity
Addition of epinephrine to local anesthetics may induce severe hypertension due to unopposed alpha action
Lidocaine with epinephrine should be avoided in patient taking antidepressant drugs such as TCA & MAOIs
Felypressin is not suitable with local anesthetics in cardiac patients

questions.text: Gingival hyperplasia is a common side effect of:
questions.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia is a common side effect of phenytoin. Option B is correct. Phenytoin's well-known side effects include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facial features, and osteomalacia. Valproate (A) causes weight gain, tremor, hepatotoxicity. Ethosuximide (C) causes GI upset, headache. Carbamazepine (D) causes SIADH, aplastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and coarse facial features through effects on connective tissue.

questions.text: The following side effect is most likely to be seen with carbamazepine
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine causes WATER RETENTION (SIADH). Option A is correct. Carbamazepine induces SIADH, causing hyponatremia and water retention. Options B, C, D are phenytoin effects (coarse facial features, hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia).
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine's SIADH effect causes dilutional hyponatremia requiring monitoring.

questions.text: Hirsutism may be induced by:
questions.explanation: Hirsutism may be induced by phenytoin. Option D is correct. Phenytoin causes hirsutism (excessive hair growth) as a characteristic side effect. Valproate (A) causes weight gain, tremor. Interferon (B) causes flu-like symptoms. Heparin (C) causes osteoporosis.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes hirsutism through altered androgen metabolism and connective tissue effects.

questions.text: Valproate toxicity does not include:
questions.explanation: Hirsutism is NOT valproate toxicity - it is caused by phenytoin. Option A is incorrect. Valproate causes hand tremor, thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity (rare but fatal). Options B, C, D are valproate toxicities. Hirsutism is a phenytoin effect.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate's main toxicities include hepatotoxicity, thrombocytopenia, and tremor; hirsutism is a phenytoin effect.

questions.text: A mood stabilizer safe in pregnant patients with bipolar depression is
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is considered safer in pregnancy. Option B is correct. Among the options, carbamazepine has better safety profile than valproate (neural tube defects) and phenytoin (fetal hydantoin syndrome). Ethosuximide is for absence seizures. However, all have teratogenic potential.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine has relatively better fetal safety profile than valproate or phenytoin.

questions.text: The following is not correctly matched to its mechanism of action:
questions.explanation: Clonazepam acts through GABA enhancement, not Cl- channel blockade - this is NOT correctly matched. Option B is incorrect. Clonazepam (benzodiazepine) enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride channel opening frequency. Sodium channel blockade (A) is phenytoin. GABA transaminase inhibition (C) is valproate. T-channel blockade (D) is ethosuximide.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines enhance GABAergic inhibition by increasing chloride channel opening frequency.

questions.text: Teratogenic effects are more likely to be induced by
questions.explanation: Teratogenic effects are most likely with valproate AND phenytoin. Option D is correct. Valproate has the HIGHEST teratogenic potential (1-2% neural tube defects). Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome. Carbamazepine has lower teratogenic risk. Both A and B are highly teratogenic.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects among antiepileptics; phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome.

questions.text: The following is not correctly matched to its mechanism of action:
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type Ca++ channels, not Na+ channels - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Ethosuximide's mechanism is T-channel blockade in thalamic neurons. Options A, B, C are correctly matched: levetiracetam binds vesicle proteins, lamotrigine blocks Na+/Ca++ channels, valproate is NMDA antagonist.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide is distinguished by T-type calcium channel blockade for absence seizures.
options: Levetiracetam/ Bind vesicle protein and modify glutamate release
Lamotrigine/ block Na+ channels & presynaptic Ca++ channels

questions.text: Ethosuximide useful in
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is useful in absence seizure. Option B is correct. Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy. It does not work for partial epilepsy (A) or tonic-clonic seizures (C). Valproate would cover both absence and tonic-clonic.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide's specificity for absence seizures comes from thalamic T-channel modulation.

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement
questions.explanation: Clonazepam is NOT 2nd line in partial epilepsy - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Carbamazepine is first-line for partial epilepsy. Clonazepam is not typically used for partial epilepsy. Options A, B, C are correct: levetiracetam and valproate are broad-spectrum, carbamazepine is first-line for partial.
questions.keyConcept: Clonazepam is reserved for absence/myoclonic seizures; carbamazepine is first-line for partial epilepsy.
options: Levetiracetam & valproate are broad spectrum used in all types of epilepsy
Carbamazepine is 1st choice in partial epilepsy
Valproate is 1st line in myoclonic epilepsy
Clonazepam is 2nd line in partial epilepsy

questions.text: Which of the following is not adverse effect of phenytoin?
questions.explanation: Agranulocytosis is NOT a phenytoin adverse effect. Option C is correct. Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, osteomalacia (via vitamin D metabolism), and teratogenicity (fetal hydantoin syndrome). Agranulocytosis is more associated with carbamazepine. Phenytoin's hematologic effects include macrocytosis and megaloblastic anemia (not agranulocytosis).
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin's adverse effects include gingival hyperplasia, osteomalacia, and teratogenicity; agranulocytosis is rare.

questions.text: Which of the following is not adverse effect of Carbamazepine?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia is NOT a carbamazepine adverse effect. Option C is correct. Carbamazepine causes agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, SIADH (dilutional hyponatremia), and is an enzyme inducer. Megaloblastic anemia is associated with phenytoin and valproate (both interfere with folate metabolism).
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes hematologic toxicity (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia) and SIADH, not megaloblastic anemia.

questions.text: The following antiepilpetic drug is not enzyme inducer
questions.explanation: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer. Option C is correct. Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor, not inducer. Phenytoin (A), carbamazepine (B), and phenobarbital (D) are all potent CYP450 inducers that increase metabolism of many drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate inhibits hepatic enzymes, unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital which are inducers.

questions.text: Regarding adverse effects & precautions with sumatriptan, which is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Sumatriptan causes hypertension, not hypotension. Option C is incorrect. Sumatriptan (5-HT1B/1D agonist) causes coronary vasoconstriction and can raise blood pressure. Options A, B, D, E are correct: bad taste, chest pressure, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, contraindicated in IHD.
questions.keyConcept: Sumatriptan's vasoconstrictor effects can cause hypertension and chest pressure; it's contraindicated in IHD.
options: Contraindicated in aptients with ischemic heart disease

questions.text: Regarding adverse effects of ergotamine, which is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Ergotamine does NOT cause hypotension. Option E is incorrect. Ergotamine causes vasoconstriction (leading to hypertension, not hypotension), nausea/vomiting, chest pressure, and with long-term use can cause valvular heart disease and peripheral vasospasm/gangrene.
questions.keyConcept: Ergotamine's vasoconstrictor properties cause hypertension and risk of gangrene, not hypotension.
options: Vasospasm & gangrene . Avoided in peripheral vascular disease
Valvular heart disease with long term use

questions.text: Which of the following drug is contraindicated during acute attack of migraine
questions.explanation: Dihydroergotamine is contraindicated during acute migraine attack (with propranolol). Option D is incorrect. Dihydroergotamine is used FOR acute attacks (not prevented). Propranolol, amitriptyline, and valproate are prophylactic agents. Combining DHE with propranolol risks hypertension due to additive vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Dihydroergotamine is a migraine abortive agent; propranolol prophylaxis combined with it risks hypertension.

questions.text: Fluoxetine does not induce:
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine does not induce marked sedation. Option D is correct. Fluoxetine is an SSRI that causes stimulation/anxiety, not sedation. It can cause nausea and anxiety. Sedation is more associated with other antidepressants (TCAs, mirtazapine). SSRIs combined with MAOIs (tranylcypromine) can cause serotonin syndrome (A is correct).
questions.keyConcept: Fluoxetine causes activating side effects (nausea, anxiety, insomnia) rather than sedation.
options: Serotonin syndrome if co- administered with tranylcypromine

questions.text: The following concerning venlafaxine is not true:
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine does NOT have frequent anticholinergic effects. Option A is incorrect. Venlafaxine (SNRI) has minimal anticholinergic activity. Nausea (C) is common, hypertension (D) can occur. It inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake (B is correct). Anticholinergic effects are characteristic of TCAs, not SNRIs.
questions.keyConcept: SNRIs like venlafaxine have minimal anticholinergic effects, unlike tricyclic antidepressants.
options: Anticholinergic side effects are frequently encountered with its use.
It is a norepinephrine serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Nausea is a troublesome side effect.

questions.text: Severe hypertension is most likely to occur following intake of old cheese with
questions.explanation: Tranylcypromine causes severe hypertensive crisis with tyramine (old cheese). Option A is correct. Tranylcypromine is a non-selective MAOI; tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, wine, fermented foods) cause hypertensive crisis. Moclobemide (B) and selegiline (C) are selective MAO-B inhibitors with less food interaction. Bupropion (D) has no MAOI activity.
questions.keyConcept: Non-selective MAOIs like tranylcypromine require tyramine-restricted diet to prevent hypertensive crisis.

questions.text: Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine but not fluoxetine because
questions.explanation: Imipramine has anticholinergic effect (treats enuresis); fluoxetine does not. Option C is correct. Nocturnal enuresis is treated with imipramine's anticholinergic effect (reduces bladder contractions). Fluoxetine has no anticholinergic activity. Both can cause insomnia (A is wrong), and imipramine is not necessarily safer than fluoxetine.
questions.keyConcept: Imipramine's anticholinergic effect reduces detrusor muscle activity, treating enuresis; fluoxetine lacks this mechanism.
options: Imipramine induces insomnia while fluoxetine induces sedation.
Imipramine possess anticholinergic effect but fluoxetine does not.

questions.text: Reduction in sexual function is least seen with
questions.explanation: Bupropion has LEAST sexual dysfunction. Option C is correct. Bupropion (NDRI) has minimal sexual side effects compared to SSRIs (fluoxetine) and TCAs (imipramine). This makes it useful when sexual dysfunction is a concern. Mirtazapine (B) also has lower sexual dysfunction than SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's dopaminergic mechanism avoids the sexual dysfunction common with serotonergic antidepressants.

questions.text: The following is not correctly matched:
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is a selective MAO-A inhibitor, not MAO-B - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Moclobemide inhibits MAO-A (preferentially metabolizes serotonin, norepinephrine). Selegiline is MAO-B selective. Options A, B, C are correctly matched: fluoxetine is SSRI, mirtazapine is alpha-2 antagonist, venlafaxine is SNRI.
questions.keyConcept: Moclobemide selectively inhibits MAO-A; selegiline at low doses is MAO-B selective.
options: Moclobemide/ selective monoamine oxidase - B inhibitor.

questions.text: Which of the following drug interaction with TCA is wrong?
questions.explanation: SSRIs INCREASE TCA toxicity, not decrease - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. SSRIs inhibit CYP450 enzymes, increasing TCA levels and toxicity. Options A, B, D are correct: alpha blockers potentiate hypotension, TCAs potentiate sympathomimetics, MAOIs cause serotonin syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs inhibit TCA metabolism via CYP450 inhibition, increasing TCA toxicity risk.
options: Alpha blocker / potential postural hypotensive effect
TCA / potentiate the effect of sympathomimitics

questions.text: The following is not adverse effect of Imipramine
questions.explanation: Convulsion is NOT an imipramine adverse effect - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Imipramine (TCA) can cause seizures, especially in overdose. Options A, B, D are correct: QT prolongation, anticholinergic effects (confusion, dry mouth, increased IOP), insomnia and hallucinations are all TCA adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: TCA overdose can cause seizures due to lowered seizure threshold and CNS toxicity.
options: Prolongation of QT interval leading to arrhythmia
Confusion, dry mouth and increase IOP

questions.text: Which of the following is not adverse effect encountered with fluoxetine?
questions.explanation: Sedation and dry mouth are NOT common with fluoxetine. Option D is incorrect. Fluoxetine causes activation (nausea, anxiety, insomnia), sexual dysfunction, and can increase suicide risk (especially in young patients). Sedation and dry mouth are characteristic of TCAs, not SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs like fluoxetine cause activating effects (nausea, insomnia, anxiety) rather than sedation.

questions.text: The following a do not induce sexual dysfunction
questions.explanation: Bupropion does NOT increase serotonin and has least sexual dysfunction. Option E is correct. Bupropion (dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) doesn't affect serotonin, avoiding sexual side effects. TCAs (A) and fluoxetine (C) cause sexual dysfunction. Mirtazapine (B) has moderate risk. Bupropion alone or with other non-serotonergic agents minimizes sexual dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's lack of serotonergic activity avoids sexual dysfunction common with other antidepressants.

questions.text: The following drug do not increase serotonin in the brain
questions.explanation: Bupropion does NOT increase serotonin in the brain. Option C is correct. Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) with no significant serotonin activity. Imipramine (A) is a TCA that blocks serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake. Fluoxetine (B) is an SSRI. Venlafaxine (D) is an SNRI. Mirtazapine (E) increases serotonin via alpha-2 blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion's mechanism involves dopamine and norepinephrine, not serotonin, distinguishing it from other antidepressants.

questions.text: Fatal dermatitis is a serious adverse effect of which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine is associated with severe dermatologic reactions including Stevens‑Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which can be fatal. These risks are dose‑dependent and higher when combined with valproate.
questions.keyConcept: Lamotrigine carries a black box warning for serious skin reactions including Stevens‑Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

questions.text: Which of the following does not have an antidote?
questions.explanation: Thiopental is a barbiturate that lacks a specific antagonist; benzodiazepines can be reversed with flumazenil. This makes barbiturate overdose management more challenging.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates such as thiopental have no specific antidote, unlike benzodiazepines which have flumazenil.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs is preferred in case of penicillin allergy in a patient with Streptococcus Pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin is the preferred alternative for serious Streptococcus pneumoniae infections in penicillin‑allergic patients, covering multi‑drug resistant strains. Cefixime is a 3rd‑generation cephalosporin (cross‑reactivity risk), rifampicin is not monotherapy, and gentamicin lacks adequate pneumococcal coverage.
questions.keyConcept: Vancomycin is the standard alternative for serious pneumococcal infections in penicillin‑allergic patients.

questions.text: Buspirone is effective in case of:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5‑HT1A partial agonist indicated specifically for generalized anxiety disorder; it has no efficacy for panic attacks (prefer benzodiazepines) or insomnia (prefer Z‑drugs).
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a first‑line treatment for generalized anxiety disorder but not for panic attacks or insomnia.

questions.text: The following anti‑epileptic drug acts by binding to SV2A to modify glutamate release:
questions.explanation: Levetiracetam selectively binds to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating calcium‑dependent neurotransmitter release and exerting its antiepileptic effect.
questions.keyConcept: Levetiracetam's antiepileptic mechanism involves SV2A binding, which modulates vesicular neurotransmitter release.

questions.text: Patient intolerant to SSRIs due to their correlation with sexual disturbances can instead take:
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine has lower rates of sexual dysfunction compared to SSRIs due to its unique alpha‑2 antagonism and 5‑HT2/5‑HT3 blocking properties, making it an alternative when sexual side effects are problematic.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine has a favorable sexual side‑effect profile compared to SSRIs.

questions.text: Moclobemide is preferred to phenelzine because:
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is a reversible, selective MAO‑A inhibitor with fewer dietary restrictions compared to non‑selective, irreversible MAO inhibitors like phenelzine.
questions.keyConcept: Moclobemide's selectivity and reversibility for MAO‑A make it safer with fewer dietary interactions than phenelzine.
options: It inhibits MAO‑A and MAO‑B enzymes
It is a selective MAO‑A inhibitor only
It can be safely used in combination with SSRIs

questions.text: Gingival hygiene and care is highly recommended when taking which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia in up to 50% of patients due to overgrowth of fibroblasts and collagen, necessitating rigorous oral hygiene and dental review.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin is notorious for causing gingival hyperplasia, requiring preventive dental care.

questions.text: The following drug is characterized by ultra‑short duration of action:
questions.explanation: Midazolam has an ultra‑short duration of action due to rapid redistribution from the brain (half‑life ~1–4 hours), making it ideal for procedural sedation.
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam's ultra‑short duration is due to rapid redistribution, not rapid metabolism.

questions.text: Flumazenil can be used as an antidote with which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines by competitive antagonism at the GABA‑A receptor; it also antagonizes z‑zolpidem and zopiclone (Z‑drugs) which act via the same receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines and Z‑drugs via competitive GABA‑A receptor blockade.

questions.text: All of the following drugs have slower onset when taken intra‑muscular except:
questions.explanation: Midazolam has rapid IM onset due to high lipid solubility and small volume of distribution; benzodiazepines like lorazepam and alprazolam have slower IM absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam has faster IM onset than other benzodiazepines due to its pharmacokinetic profile.

questions.text: Lidocaine is preferred to bupivacaine in local anesthesia due to:
questions.explanation: Lidocaine has a lower pKa (~7.9) closer to physiological pH than bupivacaine (~8.1), resulting in a higher fraction of unionized drug and faster nerve penetration and onset.
questions.keyConcept: Lidocaine's lower pKa confers faster onset compared to bupivacaine in local anesthesia.

questions.text: Chloramphenicol is the last antibiotic of choice to be used due to:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol causes dose‑dependent bone marrow suppression (reversible) and aplastic anemia ( idiosyncratic, irreversible), the latter being rare but fatal and dose‑independent.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol's most feared adverse effect is aplastic anemia, an idiosyncratic and potentially fatal bone marrow reaction.

questions.text: Dexamethasone is injected IV in meningitis for:
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone adjunctive therapy in bacterial meningitis is given as 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 2–4 days, preferably starting before or with the first dose of antibiotics.
questions.keyConcept: Dexamethasone in meningitis: 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 2–4 days, initiated with or before antibiotics.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is Wrong about using corticosteroids in meningitis?
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone should be administered before or with the first antibiotic dose; administering it after antibiotics reduces its benefit in reducing neurological complications and mortality.
questions.keyConcept: Timing is critical for dexamethasone in meningitis — it must be given before or with, not after, empiric antibiotics.
options: Should be started immediately after empiric antibiotic
May decrease penetration of vancomycin to BBB

questions.text: Which of the following is 1st choice as empiric antibiotic in meningitis suspected to be due to streptococcal Agalactiae in a 55‑year‑old patient?
questions.explanation: For a 55‑year‑old patient with suspected GBS meningitis, empiric coverage includes vancomycin (for DRSP), ceftriaxone, and ampicillin (to cover GBS and Listeria monocytogenes in patients >50 years).
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis coverage in elderly requires ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes and GBS in addition to standard vancomycin and ceftriaxone.

questions.text: Which of the following is Wrong about meningitis due to streptococcal Pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is added to vancomycin and dexamethasone because it has good CNS penetration and synergistic effects — not because it increases vancomycin metabolism. Vancomycin is primarily renally eliminated, not hepatically metabolized.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin addition in pneumococcal meningitis is for synergy and CNS penetration, not enzyme induction of vancomycin metabolism.
options: Duration of treatment up to 21 days
Ceftriaxone is chosen in ampicillin MIC >1 µg/ml
Addition of vancomycin to ceftriaxone if MIC of both Ampicillin & ceftriaxone is high
Rifampicin is added to Vancomycin during using dexamethasone because it increases metabolism of vancomycin

questions.text: Chemoprophylaxis is not recommended in meningitis due to:
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis is indicated for close contacts of meningococcal (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone) and H. influenzae type b meningitis, but NOT for pneumococcal meningitis as person‑to‑person transmission and secondary cases are not significant.
questions.keyConcept: Chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis due to lack of significant secondary transmission.

questions.text: Choose from the following pair of antibiotics not crossing BBB even if inflamed:
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B (for fungal CNS infections) and aminoglycosides have minimal BBB penetration even when the meninges are inflamed; chloramphenicol and rifampicin cross well.
questions.keyConcept: Amphotericin B and aminoglycosides are notable for poor CNS penetration even with meningeal inflammation.

questions.text: Principles of antimicrobial therapy for meningitis:
questions.explanation: Once the causative organism is identified in meningitis, antibiotic treatment duration typically ranges from 7 days (N. meningitidis) to 21 days (S. pneumoniae), depending on the pathogen and clinical response.
questions.keyConcept: Duration of meningitis treatment is pathogen‑dependent, generally 7–21 days after organism identification.
options: Antibiotics should be lipophilic‑ionized in physiological pH
Steroids should be administered after starting empiric antibiotics
Lumbar puncture should be done before choosing empiric antibiotics
Once organism is identified, treatment should be continued for 7 to 21 days

questions.text: Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 2 days is used in case of:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin prophylaxis for 2 days is used for Neisseria meningitidis, which is not listed. The other organisms listed do not have this specific 2‑day rifampicin prophylaxis regimen.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin 2‑day prophylaxis is for meningococcal contacts, but none of the listed organisms match this indication.

questions.text: Prophylaxis of close contact by rifampicin for 4 days is used in case of:
questions.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis requires rifampicin prophylaxis for 4 days for household contacts under 4 years or unvaccinated children.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin prophylaxis for 4 days is the standard for Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis contacts.

questions.text: Intrapartum Group B streptococcus prophylaxis requirements:
questions.explanation: All listed are established indications for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: GBS colonization, prior infant with GBS disease, and GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy all mandate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
questions.keyConcept: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is indicated for colonization, prior affected infant, or GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy.
options: History of delivery of infant with GBS
History of GBS bacteriuria at any time during pregnancy

questions.text: Pseudocholelithiasis is associated with:
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone causes biliary pseudolithiasis (sludge) due to precipitation with calcium in the gallbladder, which is reversible upon discontinuation. It is not true gallstones.
questions.keyConcept: Ceftriaxone forms reversible biliary pseudolithiasis by precipitating with calcium in bile.

questions.text: Prolonged QT interval is associated with:
questions.explanation: Moxifloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) is known to prolong the QT interval by blocking cardiac potassium channels (IKr), increasing the risk of Torsades de Pointes, especially in hypokalemia or concurrent QT‑prolonging drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Moxifloxacin prolongs the QT interval due to hERG potassium channel blockade, posing arrhythmia risk.

questions.text: Grey baby syndrome is associated with:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol causes gray baby syndrome in neonates due to immature hepatic glucuronidation capacity leading to drug accumulation and cardiovascular collapse.
questions.keyConcept: Gray baby syndrome is a neonate‑specific chloramphenicol toxicity due to inadequate glucuronidation and drug accumulation.

questions.text: Dexamethasone is injected intravenous for:
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone for bacterial meningitis is administered as 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 2–4 days, with the first dose given before or concurrent with antibiotics.
questions.keyConcept: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 2–4 days is the standard adjunctive regimen for bacterial meningitis.

questions.text: TB meningitis:
questions.explanation: TB meningitis requires 9–12 months of treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol ± streptomycin); ethambutol can be used, and corticosteroids (dexamethasone) are indicated in stage 2 or 3 disease.
questions.keyConcept: TB meningitis requires prolonged treatment (9–12 months) and may include ethambutol and adjunctive corticosteroids in advanced stages.
options: Corticosteroid may be required in stage 2 or 3

questions.text: Riluzole is prescribed in Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to:
questions.explanation: Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor (Na+ channel blockade) that modestly extends survival (~2–3 months) and delays ventilator dependence in ALS by reducing excitotoxic neuronal injury.
questions.keyConcept: Riluzole reduces glutamate‑mediated excitotoxicity to modestly prolong survival and delay ventilation in ALS.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding Natalizumab?
questions.explanation: Natalizumab is indicated for aggressive or relapsing‑remitting MS with high disease activity, not for mild controlled disease. It is given as monthly IV infusion and is a monoclonal antibody against α4‑integrin.
questions.keyConcept: Natalizumab is reserved for aggressive, highly active MS rather than mild disease, and reduces lymphocyte CNS invasion.
options: Indicated in mild controlled Multiple sclerosis

questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding Fingolimod?
questions.explanation: All statements are correct. Fingolimod traps T‑lymphocytes in lymph nodes (reducing CNS entry), should be used cautiously in cardiac patients (bradycardia risk), and decreases BBB invasion by T‑cells.
questions.keyConcept: Fingolimod prevents T‑lymphocyte egress from lymph nodes, reducing CNS infiltration and MS relapses.
options: Prevent T lymphocyte migration from Lymph node
Used with caution in cardiac patient

questions.text: Which of the following is correct about Fingolimod?
questions.explanation: Fingolimod was the first oral disease‑modifying therapy approved for MS and is both a sphingosine‑1‑phosphate receptor modulator that traps lymphocytes and a parenteral/neural agent with CNS effects.
questions.keyConcept: Fingolimod was the first oral disease‑modifying drug for MS and acts as a sphingosine‑1‑phosphate receptor modulator.
